empires.name: Mughal Empire
empires.intro: Founded by Babur after the first battle of Panipat, the Mughal Empire grew into one of the richest states on earth. Its emperors left behind gardens, forts, miniature paintings and the Taj Mahal, and a language, Urdu, that grew up in its camps and courts.

empires.name: Ottoman Empire
empires.intro: From a small frontier principality in Anatolia, the house of Osman built an empire that joined three continents and lasted more than six hundred years, with Istanbul as its crown.

empires.name: Roman Empire
empires.intro: Rome grew from a city of farmers on seven hills into an empire around the whole Mediterranean. Its roads, laws, language and ruins still shape the world we live in.

empires.name: Abbasid Caliphate
empires.intro: From their round city of Baghdad the Abbasid caliphs ruled an empire from North Africa to Central Asia. Their capital became the world's greatest centre of learning, where scholars translated, argued and invented for five hundred years.

empires.name: Mongol Empire
empires.intro: In a single lifetime a boy from the steppe united the Mongol tribes and built the largest land empire in history, stretching from Korea to Hungary. His heirs opened roads that carried goods, ideas and travellers across the whole of Asia.

empires.name: Delhi Sultanate
empires.intro: For three centuries five dynasties of sultans ruled northern India from Delhi. They built the Qutb Minar, held back the Mongols, welcomed poets and travellers, and laid the ground on which the Mughals would build.

empires.name: Ancient Egypt
empires.intro: For three thousand years the kingdoms of the Nile built pyramids, temples and tombs that still astonish the world. Their pharaohs ruled as gods, wrote in pictures and believed that what was built in stone would last for ever.

empires.name: Indus Valley Civilisation
empires.intro: Along the Indus and its rivers, in what is now Pakistan and north-western India, people built planned cities with drains, wells and baths more than four thousand years ago. They traded as far as Mesopotamia, and their writing has never been read.

empires.name: Al-Andalus
empires.intro: For almost eight centuries Muslim rulers governed much of Spain and Portugal. Córdoba became the largest and most learned city in western Europe, and the Alhambra of Granada still glows above the city like a memory of paradise.

empires.name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
empires.intro: Cyrus the Great and his successors built the first empire to stretch from the Indus to the Mediterranean and Egypt. They ruled dozens of peoples through governors, roads and tolerance, and left behind Persepolis, one of the wonders of the ancient world.

empires.name: Kushan Empire
empires.intro: From their capital at Peshawar the Kushan kings ruled a crossroads empire from Central Asia to the Ganges. Under them Gandhara became a meeting place of Greek, Persian, Indian and Chinese worlds, and the Buddha was carved in stone in a style the world still admires.

series.name: Babur to Akbar
series.intro: A boy king loses his homeland, crosses the mountains and founds an empire. Follow the first Mughals from the valley of Fergana to the court of Akbar the Great.

series.name: The Peacock Throne
series.intro: Jahangir, Nur Jahan, Shah Jahan and the sons who fought over his throne: the Mughal court at the height of its glory, and the family drama behind the marble.

series.name: The Rise of the Ottomans
series.intro: How a band of frontier warriors became masters of an old imperial city: from Osman's dream to the walls of Constantinople.

series.name: Suleiman the Magnificent
series.intro: The longest-reigning Ottoman sultan: lawgiver, poet and conqueror, at the height of the empire's power.

series.name: Lords of the Sea
series.intro: Two red-bearded brothers from the island of Lesbos, a silver arm, and the fleets that made the Mediterranean an Ottoman lake: the story of Barbarossa and the Ottoman navy.

series.name: From Republic to Empire
series.intro: Three turning points that ended five centuries of the Roman Republic and made one man master of the Roman world.

series.name: Pompeii: The Last Day
series.intro: A busy Roman town, a mountain no one feared, and the eruption that froze a moment of daily life for two thousand years.

series.name: The House of Wisdom
series.intro: A round city on the Tigris, a caliph who sent an elephant to Europe, and the scholars who gave the world algebra: the golden age of Baghdad, from its founding to its fall.

series.name: The Making of Genghis Khan
series.intro: An abandoned boy, a stolen bride, a great assembly and a fatal insult: how Temujin became the ruler of the world.

series.name: Sultans of Delhi
series.intro: A slave who became king, a queen who rode an elephant, a sultan who moved a whole city, and a conqueror at the gates: the stormy story of the sultans of Delhi.

series.name: Pharaohs of the Nile
series.intro: A mountain of stone, a woman who ruled as king, a pharaoh who changed the gods, a boy king's gold and the world's first peace treaty.

series.name: Cities of the Indus
series.intro: Railway bricks, a great bath, a bronze dancer and a script no one can read: the rediscovery of South Asia's first cities.

series.name: The Lights of Córdoba
series.intro: From a general who gave his name to a mountain to a king who wept for Granada: the rise and fall of al-Andalus in five episodes.

series.name: King of Kings
series.intro: Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes: how a small kingdom in southern Iran became the largest empire the world had yet seen, and how it fell to a young Macedonian.

series.name: Land of Gandhara
series.intro: Nomads from the edge of China, a great king at Peshawar, the tallest tower of its age and a Buddha in a Greek robe: the story of Gandhara under the Kushans.

episodes.title: The Prince of Fergana
episodes.excerpt: In 1494 a twelve-year-old boy inherits a small kingdom and a world of enemies.
episodes.content:
In the summer of 1494 a twelve-year-old boy named Zahir-ud-din Muhammad, remembered as Babur, the tiger, became ruler of Fergana, a green valley in Central Asia. His father had died when the dovecote he was standing on slid into a ravine.

Babur was descended from Timur on his father's side and from Genghis Khan on his mother's. Royal blood brought him no peace: uncles and cousins all wanted his throne, and twice he captured the great city of Samarkand only to lose it again.

By the time he was twenty, Babur had lost Fergana as well. He wandered the hills with a few hundred loyal men, sleeping in shepherds' tents. Yet he kept a diary, and in it he wrote that a king without a kingdom must still behave like a king.

episodes.title: The Road to Panipat
episodes.excerpt: With guns, carts and a gamble, Babur meets the Sultan of Delhi on an April morning in 1526.
episodes.content:
From Kabul, which he had taken in 1504, Babur looked east across the passes to Hindustan. Four times he raided the Punjab. In the winter of 1525 he came to stay.

On 21 April 1526 his army of perhaps twelve thousand men faced Ibrahim Lodi, Sultan of Delhi, on the plain of Panipat. Ibrahim had many times more soldiers and a thousand war elephants. Babur had something new to India: field cannon and matchlock muskets, set behind a wall of carts chained together.

By midday the battle was over. Ibrahim Lodi lay dead on the field, and within days Babur's son Humayun had ridden into Agra. A new dynasty had begun, though its founder had only four years left to live.

episodes.title: The Boy Emperor
episodes.excerpt: Crowned in a garden at thirteen, Akbar must win back an empire his father barely held.
episodes.content:
In January 1556 the emperor Humayun slipped on the stone stairs of his library in Delhi and died. His son Akbar, just thirteen, was in the Punjab, chasing rebels with his guardian Bairam Khan.

There was no palace to crown him in, so a brick platform was built in a garden at Kalanaur, and there Akbar was proclaimed emperor. Delhi itself had already fallen to Hemu, a brilliant general who now called himself king.

In November the two armies met once more at Panipat. Hemu was winning until an arrow struck him in the eye. His elephant turned, his army broke, and the boy emperor began a reign that would last almost fifty years.

episodes.title: A City of Red Sandstone
episodes.excerpt: Akbar builds a new capital on a ridge near Agra, and names it for victory.
episodes.content:
In 1569 a son was born to Akbar after long years of waiting. The emperor believed the blessing came from the Sufi saint Salim Chishti, who lived on a rocky ridge at Sikri, west of Agra.

In gratitude Akbar ordered a whole new city to be built around the saint's mosque. Palaces, courtyards, a mint and a great mosque rose in red sandstone. After his conquest of Gujarat in 1573 the city was called Fatehpur Sikri, the City of Victory.

The Buland Darwaza, the Gate of Magnificence, still towers over the town. Yet within fifteen years the court had moved on, perhaps because water was short, and the city of victory was left almost empty.

episodes.title: The Chain of Justice
episodes.excerpt: Agra, 1605: a new emperor hangs a golden chain with sixty bells, so that anyone wronged can ring for him.
episodes.content:
In October 1605 Akbar died in Agra and his son Salim took the throne under the name Jahangir, "Conqueror of the World". One of his first orders was unusual. In his memoirs he wrote that he had a chain of pure gold made, thirty gaz long and hung with sixty bells.

One end was fixed to the battlements of Agra Fort, the other to a stone post on the bank of the Yamuna. Anyone whose complaint had been ignored by the courts could pull the chain, and the bells would ring in the emperor's own chambers.

How often it was rung, no one recorded. But the chain became a symbol of how Jahangir wanted to be remembered: a ruler who loved painting, gardens and birds, and who promised his subjects that justice was only a pull away.

episodes.title: The Light of the World
episodes.excerpt: A widow from a Persian family becomes the most powerful woman the Mughal empire ever saw.
episodes.content:
Mihr-un-Nisa was born in 1577 to a Persian family travelling to India in search of fortune. Her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg, rose to high office at the Mughal court. In 1611, a widow of thirty-four, she married the emperor Jahangir.

He gave her the title Nur Mahal, then Nur Jahan, "Light of the World". Coins were struck in her name, an honour no Mughal queen had held before. Jahangir himself wrote that on one hunt she killed four tigers with six shots.

For much of the 1620s, as Jahangir's health failed, Nur Jahan was the real power behind the throne. She built a white marble tomb in Agra for her father, the Itimad-ud-Daulah. After Jahangir's death in 1627 she retired to Lahore, and she lies buried at Shahdara, close to her husband.

episodes.title: A Tomb for Mumtaz
episodes.excerpt: Burhanpur, 1631: an empress dies giving birth, and an emperor begins the most famous building on earth.
episodes.content:
Arjumand Banu Begum, niece of Nur Jahan, married Prince Khurram in 1612. When he became the emperor Shah Jahan, she was called Mumtaz Mahal, "the chosen one of the palace", and she travelled with him everywhere, even on campaign.

In June 1631, in the camp at Burhanpur in the Deccan, she died after giving birth to their fourteenth child. The court chroniclers say the emperor's beard turned white with grief and that he gave up music and fine clothes for two years.

Work on her tomb began on the bank of the Yamuna at Agra in 1632. White marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, and craftsmen inlaid it with flowers of precious stone. The mausoleum was finished around 1643 and the whole complex about ten years later. We call it the Taj Mahal.

episodes.title: The Throne of Jewels
episodes.excerpt: Seven years of goldsmiths' work, a new capital at Delhi, and a Persian king who carried it all away.
episodes.content:
In 1635 Shah Jahan sat for the first time on a throne that had taken his goldsmiths seven years to make. It was covered in gold and set with rubies, emeralds, diamonds and pearls, and on its canopy stood jewelled peacocks. People called it the Takht-e-Taus, the Peacock Throne.

In 1639 the emperor began a new capital at Delhi, Shahjahanabad, with a great fort of red sandstone on the Yamuna. When the Red Fort was finished in 1648 the Peacock Throne was placed in its Hall of Private Audience, where an inscription still reads: "If there is paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this."

Ninety years later paradise was looted. In 1739 Nadir Shah of Persia defeated the Mughal army at Karnal and entered Delhi. When he left, he took the Peacock Throne with him, along with the diamond that came to be known as the Koh-i-Noor.

episodes.title: Brothers at War
episodes.excerpt: 1658: the emperor falls ill, and four princes march on Agra.
episodes.content:
In September 1657 Shah Jahan fell seriously ill, and rumours spread that he was dead. His four sons, Dara Shikoh, Shah Shuja, Aurangzeb and Murad Bakhsh, each governed a province with an army of his own, and each knew what the rumours meant.

Dara, the eldest, was a scholar who had translated the Upanishads into Persian. Aurangzeb was a hard-headed soldier. On 29 May 1658 their armies met at Samugarh near Agra. At the height of the battle Dara climbed down from his elephant, and when his soldiers saw the empty howdah they thought he was dead and fled.

Aurangzeb took Agra and kept his father a prisoner in the fort for the last eight years of his life. Tradition says the old emperor spent his days looking out across the river at the Taj Mahal. Dara was captured and executed in 1659. The empire would reach its greatest size under Aurangzeb, and begin to crack soon after him.

episodes.title: Osman's Dream
episodes.excerpt: A frontier chief, a sheikh's daughter and a dream of a great tree.
episodes.content:
Around the year 1300 Osman was one of many Turkish chiefs on the edge of the shrinking Byzantine world in north-western Anatolia. He ruled a few villages and grazing lands near Söğüt.

Later Ottoman chroniclers told a story about him. Staying in the house of the wise Sheikh Edebali, Osman dreamed that a moon rose from the sheikh's chest and sank into his own, and from his body grew a tree whose branches covered the world.

The sheikh gave Osman his daughter in marriage. Whether or not the dream was real, Osman's small state kept growing, and his descendants would carry his name for six centuries.

episodes.title: Bursa, the First Capital
episodes.excerpt: After a long siege, Orhan takes a Byzantine city and gives the Ottomans a home.
episodes.content:
For years Ottoman warriors had surrounded the rich Byzantine city of Bursa, cutting it off from the countryside. In 1326, with no help coming from Constantinople, the city surrendered to Osman's son Orhan.

Tradition says the dying Osman heard the news before he passed away. He was buried in Bursa, and the city became the first true capital of the Ottomans.

Orhan built mosques, a market and public kitchens, and minted coins in his own name. The frontier chiefdom was turning into a state.

episodes.title: The Fall of Constantinople
episodes.excerpt: Spring 1453: a twenty-one-year-old sultan, giant cannon and ships carried over a hill.
episodes.content:
In April 1453 Sultan Mehmed II, only twenty-one years old, laid siege to Constantinople, the city that had been the capital of the Roman emperors for more than a thousand years.

Its land walls were the strongest in the world, and a great chain closed the harbour of the Golden Horn. Mehmed answered with enormous bronze cannon and, in one famous night, had his ships dragged on greased logs over the hill of Galata and into the harbour behind the chain.

On 29 May the walls were breached. The last emperor, Constantine XI, died fighting. Mehmed, now called the Conqueror, rode to the church of Hagia Sophia and made the city the new capital of his empire.

episodes.title: The Young Sultan
episodes.excerpt: September 1520: a twenty-five-year-old governor becomes master of an empire.
episodes.content:
In September 1520 Sultan Selim, feared as "the Grim", died on the road to Edirne. His only surviving son, Suleiman, was governor of Manisa, a quiet province on the Aegean coast.

Suleiman rode to Istanbul and was girded with the sword of Osman. Foreign envoys expected a gentle ruler. Within two years he had taken Belgrade and the island of Rhodes, which had resisted the Ottomans for generations.

At home his subjects would remember him by another name: Kanuni, the Lawgiver, for the codes of law his officials drew up in his name.

episodes.title: Rain at the Gates of Vienna
episodes.excerpt: 1529: the greatest army in Europe meets an enemy it cannot fight, the weather.
episodes.content:
In the spring of 1529 Suleiman marched north up the Danube with a huge army. His goal was Vienna, the city of the Habsburgs.

But it was one of the wettest summers anyone could remember. Roads turned to mud, rivers flooded, and the heavy siege cannon had to be left behind. The army reached Vienna only in late September.

For three weeks the Ottomans dug mines under the walls, and the defenders dug countermines. With winter coming and supplies running out, Suleiman ordered the retreat. Vienna had survived, and the high tide of the Ottoman advance into Europe had been marked.

episodes.title: The Architect Sinan
episodes.excerpt: A boy taken from a Christian village becomes the greatest builder in Ottoman history.
episodes.content:
Sinan was born around 1490 in a Christian village in Anatolia and was taken into the sultan's service through the devshirme, the levy of boys trained for the army and the palace. He became a Janissary engineer, building bridges and boats on campaign.

In 1538, already in his late forties, he was appointed chief royal architect. For the next fifty years he and his office designed hundreds of buildings across the empire: mosques, schools, hospitals, bridges, baths and caravanserais.

His masterpiece for Suleiman, the Süleymaniye Mosque, was built on a hill above the Golden Horn between 1550 and 1557. Its great dome still rules the Istanbul skyline. Suleiman and his wife Hürrem are buried in its garden, and Sinan, who lived to nearly a hundred, lies in a modest tomb just outside its walls.

episodes.title: The Brothers from Lesbos
episodes.excerpt: Two sons of a potter become the most feared sailors in the Mediterranean.
episodes.content:
In the late fifteenth century, on the Aegean island of Lesbos, which the Turks called Midilli, lived a former Ottoman soldier named Yakup who had settled there as a potter. Two of his sons, Oruç and Hızır, went to sea as young men, trading and then raiding along the coasts.

In the early 1500s the brothers moved their base to North Africa. As Spain drove out its Muslims, they used their ships to carry thousands of refugees from Andalusia to safety, and grateful Muslims called Oruç "Baba Oruç", Father Oruç. Europeans, struck by his red beard, called him Barbarossa.

In 1512, attacking the Spanish-held port of Bougie in Algeria, Oruç was hit by a shot that shattered his arm, and it had to be amputated. Legend says he had an arm made of silver and went on fighting. The brothers were becoming a power that no one on the sea could ignore.

episodes.title: The Keys of Algiers
episodes.excerpt: Oruç dies fighting the Spanish, and his brother makes a bold offer to the Ottoman sultan.
episodes.content:
In 1516 Oruç took control of Algiers, then a small port threatened by a Spanish fortress built on an island in its harbour. He made himself its ruler and expanded inland, but in 1518 the Spanish caught him near Tlemcen and he was killed in battle.

His younger brother Hızır, now known as Hayreddin, was left alone against Spain and hostile local rulers. He made a decision that changed the history of North Africa: he offered Algiers to the Ottoman sultan Selim I. The sultan accepted, made Hayreddin governor, and sent him Janissaries and cannon.

In 1529 Hayreddin finally captured the Spanish fortress on the island, the Peñón, and used its stones to build a breakwater joining the island to the shore. That gave Algiers a safe harbour, and for the next three centuries it was one of the great naval bases of the Mediterranean.

episodes.title: The Grand Admiral
episodes.excerpt: 1533: Suleiman summons the old corsair to Istanbul and hands him the Ottoman fleet.
episodes.content:
By the 1530s the Ottomans faced a powerful enemy at sea: Andrea Doria, the Genoese admiral serving the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. Suleiman the Magnificent needed a commander who knew the western Mediterranean, and in 1533 he summoned Hayreddin to Istanbul.

The sultan made him Kapudan Pasha, grand admiral of the Ottoman navy, and governor of the islands. Hayreddin, now in his sixties, threw himself into rebuilding the fleet in the arsenal on the Golden Horn, where dozens of new galleys were launched.

In 1534 he seized Tunis, but the next year Charles V led a huge expedition and took it back. Hayreddin escaped to Algiers, gathered his ships and raided the coasts of Spain and Italy. The struggle for the Mediterranean was just beginning.

episodes.title: The Battle of Preveza
episodes.excerpt: September 1538: Barbarossa's smaller fleet meets the combined navies of Christian Europe.
episodes.content:
In 1538 the Pope, Venice and Charles V formed a Holy League and gathered a great fleet under Andrea Doria, larger than anything Hayreddin could put to sea. The Ottoman fleet waited in the Gulf of Preveza, on the western coast of Greece.

On 28 September Doria's fleet appeared outside the gulf. Hayreddin came out to meet it. The allied commanders did not trust one another, the wind fell, and Doria hesitated to commit his ships. Hayreddin's galleys attacked, captured or sank a number of enemy ships, and by nightfall Doria withdrew.

Preveza gave the Ottomans control of the eastern Mediterranean for more than thirty years. Hayreddin died in Istanbul in 1546 and was buried in a tomb on the shore at Beşiktaş, and for generations Ottoman ships fired a salute as they passed it. The Turkish navy still marks its Navy Day each September in memory of the battle.

episodes.title: Lepanto and the Shaved Beard
episodes.excerpt: 1571: the Ottoman fleet is destroyed in a single day, and a vizier explains why it does not matter.
episodes.content:
In 1570 the Ottomans invaded Cyprus, then ruled by Venice. In response the Pope, Spain and Venice formed a new Holy League, and on 7 October 1571 its fleet, commanded by the young Don John of Austria, met the Ottoman fleet under Müezzinzade Ali Pasha at the mouth of the Gulf of Lepanto, further down the same coast from Preveza.

It was one of the largest sea battles ever fought with oared galleys. The allied ships carried more guns and more soldiers with firearms, and by evening most of the Ottoman fleet had been captured or sunk and Ali Pasha was dead. Among the wounded Spaniards was a young soldier named Miguel de Cervantes, who lost the use of his left hand and later wrote Don Quixote.

Europe celebrated, but the grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha told the Venetian envoy: by taking Cyprus we cut off your arm; by defeating our fleet you only shaved our beard, and a shaved beard grows back thicker. Over the following winter the Ottoman arsenals built a new fleet, and in 1573 Venice gave up Cyprus.

episodes.title: Crossing the Rubicon
episodes.excerpt: January 49 BC: a general reaches a small river and makes a choice there is no coming back from.
episodes.content:
In January 49 BC Julius Caesar, governor of Gaul, stood with a single legion beside the Rubicon, a small river that marked the border of Italy. The Senate had ordered him to give up his army. Crossing the river under arms would mean civil war.

According to the historian Suetonius, Caesar hesitated, then said: "The die is cast." His soldiers followed him across.

Rome's greatest general, Pompey, fled the city with much of the Senate. Within four years Caesar had defeated his rivals from Greece to Egypt to Spain.

episodes.title: The Ides of March
episodes.excerpt: 15 March 44 BC: the dictator for life walks into a meeting of the Senate.
episodes.content:
By 44 BC Caesar had been named dictator for life. To many senators this was a king in all but name, and Rome had sworn never to have a king again.

On the Ides of March, the fifteenth day of the month, Caesar went to a meeting of the Senate in the theatre of Pompey. A group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius surrounded him and stabbed him twenty-three times.

The conspirators thought they were saving the Republic. Instead the city fell into another round of civil war, and Caesar's young adopted son, Octavian, stepped forward to claim his inheritance.

episodes.title: Augustus, the First Emperor
episodes.excerpt: He never called himself king, yet he ruled Rome for forty years.
episodes.content:
After defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, Octavian was the only power left in the Roman world. He was careful not to repeat Caesar's mistakes.

In 27 BC he announced that he was handing the Republic back to the Senate and the people. The grateful Senate gave him the name Augustus, "the revered one", and asked him to keep command of most of the armies.

He called himself only princeps, the first citizen. But from then until his death in AD 14, Augustus held power over everything that mattered, and the Roman Empire had begun.

episodes.title: A Town Beneath the Mountain
episodes.excerpt: Bakeries, taverns and election slogans: ordinary life in Pompeii.
episodes.content:
Pompeii was a prosperous town of perhaps eleven thousand people on the Bay of Naples. Its streets were lined with bakeries, laundries, taverns and fast-food counters, and its walls were painted with election slogans.

Above the town rose Vesuvius, green with vineyards. Nobody thought of it as a volcano. In AD 62 a strong earthquake damaged many buildings, and seventeen years later the builders were still repairing them.

The townspeople did not know that the earthquake was a warning.

episodes.title: The Cloud Shaped Like a Pine
episodes.excerpt: AD 79: a young man across the bay watches the mountain explode, and writes it all down.
episodes.content:
Around midday the mountain burst open. Across the bay, seventeen-year-old Pliny the Younger saw a huge cloud rising, shaped, he wrote, like an umbrella pine.

His uncle, Pliny the Elder, commander of the fleet, sailed toward the coast to rescue people and never came back. In Pompeii, ash and pumice fell for hours, roofs collapsed, and the next morning surges of burning gas swept through the streets.

The town lay buried and forgotten for more than sixteen centuries. When excavators found it, the hollows left by the victims in the ash allowed them to make plaster casts of the last moments of the people of Pompeii.

episodes.title: The Round City
episodes.excerpt: 762: a caliph chooses a spot on the Tigris and draws a perfect circle.
episodes.content:
In 762 the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur went looking for a site for a new capital. He chose a village on the west bank of the Tigris, where the river came closest to the Euphrates and boats could arrive from Basra, Syria and Persia.

His city was built as a perfect circle, with double walls and four gates named after the roads they faced: Kufa, Basra, Khurasan and Syria. At its centre stood the caliph's palace, crowned by a green dome, and beside it the great mosque. He named it Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, but everyone called it Baghdad.

Tens of thousands of workers built it in about four years. Within a generation the city had spilled far beyond its walls, and Baghdad was on its way to becoming one of the largest cities in the world.

episodes.title: An Elephant for Charlemagne
episodes.excerpt: 802: a white elephant named Abul-Abbas walks into a Frankish palace.
episodes.content:
Harun al-Rashid became caliph in 786 and ruled for twenty-three years. Later storytellers made his court the setting of the Thousand and One Nights, but the real Baghdad of his day was rich enough without any magic: silk, paper, spices and scholars flowed into it from every direction.

Far to the west, the Frankish king Charlemagne sent envoys to the caliph. When they returned, they brought a gift that Europe had not seen in centuries: an elephant. The Frankish royal annals record that in July 802 the elephant, named Abul-Abbas, arrived at Charlemagne's court in Aachen.

Charlemagne kept the elephant for eight years and took it with him on his travels. A few years later another embassy brought a brass water clock that struck the hours by dropping metal balls onto a cymbal. The Franks had never seen anything like it.

episodes.title: The House of Wisdom
episodes.excerpt: Under the caliph al-Ma'mun, Baghdad sets out to translate the knowledge of the whole world.
episodes.content:
Al-Ma'mun, a son of Harun, became caliph in 813. He was fascinated by philosophy and science, and he supported a palace library and academy known as the Bayt al-Hikma, the House of Wisdom.

Scholars there translated works of Greek philosophy, medicine, astronomy and mathematics into Arabic, along with books from Persian and Sanskrit. The most famous translator, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian doctor, was said to be paid in gold by the weight of the books he translated. Cheap paper, made in Baghdad's mills, let the new books spread quickly.

Al-Ma'mun also sent astronomers into the desert plain of Sinjar to measure the length of one degree of the earth's surface, and so the size of the earth itself. Their answer was remarkably close. Many Greek works survive today only because they were copied in Baghdad.

episodes.title: The Father of Algebra
episodes.excerpt: A scholar from Khwarazm writes a book on "completing and balancing", and two new words enter the world.
episodes.content:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi came from Khwarazm, the land around the Aral Sea, and worked in Baghdad in the time of al-Ma'mun. Around 820 he wrote a short book on solving equations, which he called the Book of Calculation by Completion and Balancing.

The word for "completion" in its title was al-jabr. When the book was translated into Latin in the twelfth century, that word became "algebra". His method was meant to be practical: he used it to solve problems of inheritance, trade and land measurement.

He also wrote a book explaining the Indian way of writing numbers with nine digits and a zero. In Latin his name became Algoritmi, and from it comes the word "algorithm", which today runs every computer and phone on earth.

episodes.title: The Tigris Runs Black
episodes.excerpt: February 1258: the Mongols reach Baghdad, and five centuries of the caliphate end in a week.
episodes.content:
By the 1250s the Abbasid caliphs had lost most of their real power, but Baghdad was still a great city and the caliph was still the symbol of the Sunni Muslim world. In 1257 the Mongol prince Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, demanded that the caliph al-Musta'sim submit to him. The caliph refused.

In January 1258 the Mongol armies surrounded the city and battered its walls with siege engines. On 10 February the caliph surrendered. For about a week the Mongols plundered Baghdad and killed a great part of its people.

The caliph himself was put to death; one account says he was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses, so that no royal blood would touch the ground. Later writers said the Tigris ran black with the ink of books thrown into it from the city's libraries. The golden age of Baghdad was over.

episodes.title: A Boy Called Temujin
episodes.excerpt: The steppe, around 1170: a chief is poisoned and his family is left alone to starve.
episodes.content:
Temujin was born around 1162 beside the Onon River in what is now Mongolia. The Secret History of the Mongols, written soon after his death, says he came into the world clutching a clot of blood in his fist, a sign that he would be a great warrior.

When he was about nine, his father Yesügei was poisoned by Tatars while sharing their meal on the road. Without its chief, the clan abandoned his widow Hö'elün and her children on the open steppe.

The family survived by gathering roots and berries and catching fish and marmots. Hö'elün taught her sons that they had no friends but their own shadows. The hunger and humiliation of those years shaped the man Temujin would become.

episodes.title: The Rescue of Börte
episodes.excerpt: Raiders carry off Temujin's young wife, and he gathers his first army to bring her back.
episodes.content:
When Temujin was a boy his father had arranged his marriage to Börte, the daughter of a chief of the Onggirat tribe. Years later, as a young man with almost nothing, he went back to claim her, and her family kept their word.

Soon afterwards, Merkit raiders attacked the camp at dawn. Temujin escaped into the mountains, but Börte was carried off. It was the old revenge of the steppe: long ago, Temujin's own father had taken his mother from a Merkit.

Temujin turned to Toghrul, khan of the powerful Kereits and an old friend of his father, and to his blood brother Jamukha. With their warriors he raided the Merkit camp and found Börte in the darkness. She remained his chief wife for the rest of his life, and the mother of his four heirs.

episodes.title: The Great Assembly
episodes.excerpt: 1206: on the banks of the Onon, the tribes of the steppe raise a white banner and name a universal ruler.
episodes.content:
Over twenty years of war, Temujin defeated every rival on the steppe, including his old ally Toghrul and his blood brother Jamukha. In the spring of 1206 the Mongol nobles met in a great assembly, a kurultai, near the source of the Onon River.

There they raised a white banner with nine tails and proclaimed Temujin as Chinggis Khan, a title usually understood to mean "universal" or "fierce" ruler. The many tribes of the steppe were now one people: the Mongols.

Chinggis organised his army into units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, deliberately mixing men from different tribes so that loyalty to the khan would come before loyalty to the clan. He also ordered that the Mongol language be written down, using the script of the Uyghurs.

episodes.title: The Caravan at Otrar
episodes.excerpt: 1218: a governor murders a caravan of merchants, and the Mongols turn west.
episodes.content:
Chinggis Khan wanted trade with the rich Khwarazmian empire, which ruled Central Asia and Persia. In 1218 he sent a caravan of several hundred merchants to the border city of Otrar. Its governor, Inalchuq, accused them of being spies and had them killed.

Chinggis sent envoys to Shah Muhammad II of Khwarazm to demand justice. The shah had one envoy killed and the others' beards shaved off, a deadly insult. In 1219 the Mongol armies crossed the mountains.

Otrar, Bukhara and Samarkand fell one after another. The shah fled and died on an island in the Caspian Sea. His son Jalal ad-Din fought on, and in 1221, beaten on the bank of the Indus, he is said to have ridden his horse off a high bank into the river and swum to safety. Watching him, Chinggis reportedly told his sons that every father should wish for such a son.

episodes.title: A Grave No One Can Find
episodes.excerpt: August 1227: the conqueror dies on campaign, and his burial place vanishes from history.
episodes.content:
In 1226 Chinggis Khan, now in his sixties, led his armies against the Tangut kingdom of Western Xia, in what is now north-western China. The Tangut had refused to send troops for his western war, and he meant to punish them.

During the campaign, in August 1227, he died. The sources do not agree on how: a fall from his horse during a hunt, an illness, or simply age and exhaustion. His body was carried back to Mongolia, to the sacred lands near the mountain of Burkhan Khaldun.

Where exactly he was buried no one knows. Later stories say that everyone who saw the funeral procession was killed and that horses were driven over the grave to hide it. Expeditions still search for it today. His son Ögedei was chosen as the next Great Khan, and the empire kept growing for another fifty years.

episodes.title: The Slave Who Became King
episodes.excerpt: Lahore, 1206: a Turkish slave-general becomes the first sultan of Delhi, and dies four years later in a game of polo.
episodes.content:
Qutb-ud-din Aibak was born in Central Asia and sold as a boy into slavery. He was bought by Muhammad of Ghor, the sultan who conquered much of northern India in the 1190s, and rose to become his most trusted general.

When Muhammad of Ghor was murdered in 1206, Aibak was crowned in Lahore as an independent ruler. Because he and several of the sultans after him had begun life as slaves, his line is often called the Slave dynasty. In Delhi he began a great mosque and, beside it, a victory tower that his successor Iltutmish completed: the Qutb Minar.

Aibak ruled for only four years. In 1210, while playing chaugan, the polo of the time, in Lahore, he fell from his horse and was killed. His tomb still stands in Anarkali, in the heart of old Lahore.

episodes.title: Razia Sultan
episodes.excerpt: 1236: for the first and only time, a woman sits on the throne of Delhi.
episodes.content:
The sultan Iltutmish had several sons, but he named his daughter Razia as his heir, saying she was more capable than any of them. After his death in 1236 the nobles first crowned her brother Ruknuddin, but he was so careless that within months they replaced him with Razia.

Razia set aside the veil, dressed in a tunic and cap like a man, and rode on an elephant through the streets so that her people could see her. She held court in person and led her armies herself. The historian Minhaj-us-Siraj, who knew her, called her a great sovereign, wise, just and generous.

But the powerful Turkish nobles, known as the Forty, resented her, especially her favour to an Abyssinian officer, Jamal-ud-din Yaqut. In 1240 the governor of Bathinda, Altunia, rebelled and captured her. Razia married Altunia and marched with him to win back her throne, but both were defeated and killed near Kaithal.

episodes.title: Prices in the Market
episodes.excerpt: Alauddin Khalji holds back the Mongols and fixes the price of every sack of grain in Delhi.
episodes.content:
Alauddin Khalji seized the throne in 1296 after murdering his uncle, the sultan Jalaluddin. It was a bloody start, but his reign of twenty years would be one of the strongest the sultanate ever had.

Again and again Mongol armies rode down from Afghanistan, and in 1303 they camped outside Delhi itself. Alauddin beat them back and built a new fortified city, Siri, to protect the capital. To pay a huge standing army without raising salaries, he did something remarkable: he fixed the prices of grain, cloth, horses and almost everything sold in Delhi's markets.

The historian Ziauddin Barani describes government stores of grain, inspectors in the markets and spies reporting cheating shopkeepers, who were punished severely. Prices, he says, stayed steady even in years of drought. In 1311 Alauddin added a beautiful domed gateway to the Qutb mosque, the Alai Darwaza, which still stands.

episodes.title: A Capital on the Move
episodes.excerpt: 1327: the most brilliant and unpredictable of the sultans orders all of Delhi to move 1,100 kilometres south.
episodes.content:
Muhammad bin Tughlaq, who came to the throne in 1325, was one of the most learned rulers of his age, a scholar of philosophy, poetry and medicine. He was also famous for plans that were far ahead of their time and often ended in disaster.

In 1327 he decided that his capital should be closer to the centre of his empire. He chose Devagiri in the Deccan, renamed it Daulatabad, and ordered much of Delhi's population to move there, a journey of more than a thousand kilometres. Many died on the road, and after a few years the court moved back.

He also issued coins of copper and brass that were meant to be worth the same as silver ones. Within a short time every house had become a mint, and the forged coins had to be bought back. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who served this sultan as a judge in Delhi, wrote that he was the most generous of men and also the most eager to shed blood.

episodes.title: Timur at the Gates
episodes.excerpt: December 1398: a lame conqueror from Samarkand crosses the Indus, and Delhi pays the price.
episodes.content:
By the 1390s the Tughlaq sultanate was weak and divided, with rival sultans and quarrelling nobles. Far to the north-west, in Samarkand, the conqueror Timur, known in Europe as Tamerlane, saw an opportunity.

In 1398 Timur crossed the Indus and marched through the Punjab. On 17 December he defeated the army of Sultan Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq outside Delhi. His soldiers had been terrified of the sultan's war elephants, so Timur scattered iron caltrops on the ground and, according to later accounts, drove camels loaded with burning straw at the beasts.

Timur entered Delhi, and for several days his army plundered the city. When he left early the next year he took thousands of craftsmen back to Samarkand to build his great mosque there. The sultanate never fully recovered, and little more than a century later Timur's descendant Babur would come down the same road to found the Mughal Empire.

episodes.title: A Mountain of Stone
episodes.excerpt: Giza, around 2560 BC: how a king's tomb became the tallest building on earth for nearly four thousand years.
episodes.content:
The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC. It is made of about 2.3 million blocks of stone and originally stood about 146 metres tall. For nearly four thousand years nothing built by human hands was taller.

It was not built by slaves, as old stories claimed. Archaeologists have found the village where the workers lived, with bakeries, breweries and cemeteries where they were buried with honour near the king they served. Many were farmers who worked in teams and rotated in and out.

In 2013 archaeologists found the oldest inscribed papyri in Egypt at the Red Sea harbour of Wadi al-Jarf. They include the logbook of an official named Merer, who recorded how his team of about forty men ferried blocks of fine white limestone down the Nile to Giza for the Great Pyramid.

episodes.title: The Woman Who Was King
episodes.excerpt: Hatshepsut rules Egypt for twenty years as pharaoh, false beard and all, and sends ships to the land of Punt.
episodes.content:
When the pharaoh Thutmose II died around 1479 BC, his heir Thutmose III was a small child. His stepmother and aunt, Hatshepsut, became regent. Within a few years she did something almost unheard of: she had herself crowned as pharaoh.

Her statues often show her in the clothes of a male king, with the royal false beard. Her reign of about twenty years was peaceful and rich. She built a magnificent terraced temple at Deir el-Bahari, and on its walls she recorded a great expedition by ship to the land of Punt, which brought back incense trees, ebony, gold and exotic animals.

After her death Thutmose III ruled for many years. Late in his reign, many of her statues were smashed and her name was cut from monuments, perhaps to make his own succession look smoother. For centuries she was almost forgotten, until archaeologists pieced her story back together.

episodes.title: The Pharaoh Who Changed the Gods
episodes.excerpt: Akhenaten turns his back on Egypt's ancient gods and builds a new city in the desert for the sun.
episodes.content:
Amenhotep IV came to the throne around 1353 BC, heir to an empire at the height of its wealth. Within a few years he had done something no pharaoh had done before. He raised one god, the Aten, the disc of the sun, above all the others, and changed his own name to Akhenaten, "effective for the Aten".

He built a new capital in the desert halfway between Thebes and Memphis and called it Akhetaten, "Horizon of the Aten". Its temples had no roofs, so that the sun's rays could fall directly on the altars. Art changed too: the king and his queen, Nefertiti, were shown playing with their daughters in scenes of family life.

The revolution did not outlast him. After his death around 1336 BC the old gods returned, the new city was abandoned, and later kings tried to erase his memory. The site, known today as Amarna, has given archaeologists a rare picture of a whole Egyptian city.

episodes.title: Wonderful Things
episodes.excerpt: November 1922: a candle flickers in a dark doorway, and the world meets Tutankhamun.
episodes.content:
Tutankhamun became pharaoh as a boy of about nine, soon after the reign of Akhenaten, and died around 1323 BC at about nineteen. He was a minor king, and his small tomb in the Valley of the Kings was soon buried under the rubble of later building work and forgotten.

The English archaeologist Howard Carter searched the valley for years, paid by Lord Carnarvon. On 4 November 1922 his workers uncovered a step cut into the rock. On 26 November Carter made a small hole in a sealed doorway and held up a candle. Carnarvon asked if he could see anything. "Yes," Carter replied, "wonderful things."

The tomb held more than five thousand objects: chariots, beds, jewellery, weapons, games and statues. In 1925 Carter opened the innermost coffin, made of solid gold, and found the king's mummy wearing the golden mask that is now the most famous object from ancient Egypt.

episodes.title: The First Peace Treaty
episodes.excerpt: Ramesses II fights the Hittites at Kadesh, claims a great victory, and then signs the oldest peace treaty we have.
episodes.content:
Around 1274 BC the young pharaoh Ramesses II marched into Syria to fight the Hittite empire for the city of Kadesh. The Hittite king Muwatalli II had hidden his chariots behind the city, and they fell on the Egyptian army while it was still on the march.

Ramesses fought his way out of the trap, and back in Egypt he had the battle carved on temple walls as a glorious victory. In fact neither side won, and Kadesh stayed in Hittite hands.

About fifteen years later Ramesses and the new Hittite king, Hattusili III, agreed a treaty of peace and alliance. Copies survive in Egyptian hieroglyphs on temple walls and in Akkadian on clay tablets found in the Hittite capital. It is the oldest surviving peace treaty in the world, and a replica hangs today at the United Nations in New York.

episodes.title: Bricks for the Railway
episodes.excerpt: 1850s: engineers building a railway in the Punjab find an endless supply of ancient bricks.
episodes.content:
In the 1850s British engineers were building the railway line between Lahore and Multan. They needed ballast for the track, and near the village of Harappa they found mounds full of old, well-baked bricks. Cartloads were taken away and laid under the rails.

Nobody knew how old the bricks were. In the 1870s the archaeologist Alexander Cunningham found a small stone seal at Harappa carved with a bull and signs in an unknown script, but he thought it had come from somewhere else.

Real excavation began in 1921 at Harappa under Daya Ram Sahni, and in 1922 R. D. Banerji began digging at Mohenjo-daro in Sindh. On 20 September 1924 Sir John Marshall announced in the Illustrated London News that a lost civilisation, as old as those of Egypt and Mesopotamia, had been found along the Indus.

episodes.title: The Great Bath
episodes.excerpt: Mohenjo-daro, 2500 BC: a city of straight streets, covered drains and a pool sealed with tar.
episodes.content:
Mohenjo-daro, near Larkana in Sindh, was one of the largest cities of its time, home to perhaps forty thousand people around 2500 BC. Its streets were laid out in a grid, and almost every house had its own bathing area connected to covered brick drains that ran beneath the streets.

On the raised mound of the citadel stands the Great Bath, a pool about twelve metres long, seven wide and over two metres deep. Its bricks were fitted tightly and sealed with a layer of natural tar to keep the water in. Steps lead down into it from both ends.

No one knows exactly what it was used for, though many scholars think it was for ritual bathing. The city also had hundreds of brick-lined wells. Mohenjo-daro was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.

episodes.title: The Dancer and the Priest-King
episodes.excerpt: Two small figures from Mohenjo-daro become the faces of a vanished people.
episodes.content:
In 1926 the archaeologist Ernest Mackay found a bronze figure about ten centimetres tall in a house at Mohenjo-daro. It shows a slender young woman, her left arm covered in bangles, one hand on her hip, standing with confidence. She became known as the Dancing Girl.

A year later, in 1927, excavators found a bearded man carved in soft white stone, wearing a band around his forehead and a cloak decorated with trefoil patterns that once held red paint. Archaeologists named him the Priest-King, although no one knows whether he was either.

The two figures were separated when the subcontinent was divided in 1947. The Dancing Girl is in the National Museum in New Delhi, and the Priest-King is in the National Museum of Pakistan in Karachi. Both are among the most famous works of art from the ancient world.

episodes.title: A Script No One Can Read
episodes.excerpt: Thousands of tiny seals, hundreds of signs, ships from Meluhha, and a language still waiting to be heard.
episodes.content:
The people of the Indus cities wrote. Their signs appear on thousands of small square seals of carved stone, often above the figure of an animal such as a bull, an elephant or a one-horned creature that archaeologists call the unicorn. Scholars count around four hundred different signs.

But the inscriptions are very short, usually about five signs, and no long text or bilingual inscription has ever been found. Without one, no one has been able to decipher the script, and we do not even know what language its writers spoke.

We do know they travelled. Indus seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia, in modern Iraq, and Mesopotamian texts speak of a distant land called Meluhha that sent carnelian, timber and ivory by sea. King Sargon of Akkad boasted around 2300 BC that ships from Meluhha docked at his capital. Most historians believe Meluhha was the Indus.

episodes.title: When the Rivers Moved
episodes.excerpt: Around 1900 BC the great cities begin to empty. Was it war, or the weather?
episodes.content:
For seven centuries the Indus cities flourished. Then, from around 1900 BC, things began to change. The great cities shrank, the seals and the writing slowly disappeared, and people moved to smaller villages further east and south.

For a long time the favourite explanation was invasion. In the 1940s the archaeologist Mortimer Wheeler pointed to skeletons in the streets of Mohenjo-daro as victims of a massacre. Later study showed that the skeletons came from different periods, and most historians no longer believe a single invasion ended the civilisation.

Today scientists point instead to a changing climate. The monsoon rains weakened over several centuries, and rivers shifted course. The Ghaggar-Hakra river, along which many towns stood, dried up. The people of the Indus did not vanish; their villages, crafts and perhaps some of their beliefs lived on in the cultures that followed.

episodes.title: The Mountain of Tariq
episodes.excerpt: 711: a Berber general crosses a narrow strait, and a rock is named after him for ever.
episodes.content:
In the spring of 711 a Berber commander named Tariq ibn Ziyad, serving the Umayyad governor of North Africa, Musa ibn Nusayr, crossed the narrow strait between Africa and Spain with an army of about seven thousand men. He landed beside a great rock.

The rock was named Jabal Tariq, the Mountain of Tariq, and in time the name became Gibraltar. A famous later story says Tariq burned his ships so his men could not retreat, but the earliest historians do not mention it, and it is probably a legend.

In July 711 Tariq met Roderic, the Visigothic king of Spain, near the Guadalete river and defeated him; the king was never seen again. Within a few years most of the Iberian peninsula was under Muslim rule, and the land they called al-Andalus had been born.

episodes.title: The Falcon of the Quraysh
episodes.excerpt: 750: the last Umayyad prince swims the Euphrates to escape a massacre, and rebuilds his dynasty at the other end of the world.
episodes.content:
In 750 the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyad caliphs of Damascus and hunted down their family. A twenty-year-old prince, Abd al-Rahman, escaped. With his younger brother he plunged into the Euphrates as soldiers closed in. Abd al-Rahman reached the far bank; his brother turned back, trusting a promise of safety, and was killed.

For five years Abd al-Rahman wandered across North Africa, often in disguise. His mother was a Berber, and her people helped him. In 755 he landed in Spain, and in 756 he took Córdoba and was proclaimed emir.

His dynasty would rule al-Andalus for more than two centuries. Even his enemy, the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur, admired him and called him the Falcon of the Quraysh. Homesick for Syria, Abd al-Rahman planted a palm tree in his garden at Córdoba and wrote a poem to it, a stranger far from home like himself.

episodes.title: A Forest of Columns
episodes.excerpt: Córdoba, 785: a mosque begins that will grow for two centuries into a forest of red and white arches.
episodes.content:
In 785 Abd al-Rahman I began building a great mosque in Córdoba. His successors enlarged it again and again over the next two hundred years, until it was one of the largest mosques in the world.

Inside, hundreds of columns of marble, jasper and granite, many taken from older Roman and Visigothic buildings, hold up double tiers of arches striped in red brick and white stone. Walking among them feels like walking through a forest of palm trees. In the tenth century the caliph al-Hakam II added a mihrab glittering with gold mosaics made by craftsmen sent from Constantinople.

In 1236 King Ferdinand III of Castile captured Córdoba, and the mosque was consecrated as a cathedral. In the sixteenth century a tall Renaissance nave was built in its middle. When the emperor Charles V saw it, he is said to have remarked that they had built something that could be found anywhere and destroyed something that was unique in the world.

episodes.title: The City of the Caliph
episodes.excerpt: 929: an emir declares himself caliph, and builds a palace-city of marble in the hills above Córdoba.
episodes.content:
Abd al-Rahman III came to power in 912 in a divided and rebellious al-Andalus, and spent years bringing it back under control. In 929 he took a bold step: he declared himself caliph, a title equal to that of the Abbasids in Baghdad and the Fatimids in North Africa.

From about 936 he built a magnificent palace-city in the foothills outside Córdoba, called Madinat al-Zahra. Visiting ambassadors from Constantinople and the German emperor were received in halls of marble and gold. Córdoba itself was then one of the largest cities in Europe, and the library of his son al-Hakam II was said to hold some four hundred thousand books.

The glory did not last. In 1010, during a civil war, Madinat al-Zahra was sacked and abandoned, and its stones were carried off for other buildings. Excavations began in 1911, and in 2018 the ruins became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

episodes.title: The Last Sigh of the Moor
episodes.excerpt: 2 January 1492: the keys of Granada are handed over, and a king looks back from a mountain pass.
episodes.content:
By the fifteenth century only one Muslim kingdom was left in Spain: the Nasrid emirate of Granada, protected by mountains and crowned by the red palace of the Alhambra. In 1482 the united crowns of Castile and Aragon, under Ferdinand and Isabella, began a war to conquer it.

Town by town the kingdom shrank, and in 1491 the city of Granada itself was besieged. Its young sultan, Muhammad XII, known to the Spanish as Boabdil, negotiated a surrender that promised Muslims the right to keep their religion and laws. On 2 January 1492 he handed over the keys of the city.

A famous legend says that as Boabdil rode into exile he stopped on a mountain pass, looked back at Granada and wept, and his mother told him to weep like a woman for what he could not defend like a man. The pass is still called the Last Sigh of the Moor. The promises of the surrender were broken within a few years.

episodes.title: Cyrus Enters Babylon
episodes.excerpt: 539 BC: the greatest city on earth opens its gates, and a clay cylinder records the king's promises.
episodes.content:
Cyrus II, a prince of the small kingdom of Anshan in southern Iran, defeated the Medes around 550 BC and then the rich kingdom of Lydia in Anatolia. In October 539 BC his army entered Babylon, the greatest city of the age, largely without a fight.

Cyrus presented himself not as a conqueror but as a liberator chosen by Babylon's own god, Marduk. He allowed peoples deported by the Babylonian kings to go home and rebuild their temples. Among them were the Jews, and the Bible remembers Cyrus with unusual honour.

In 1879 the archaeologist Hormuzd Rassam found a barrel-shaped clay cylinder in the ruins of Babylon. Written in Babylonian cuneiform, it tells Cyrus's version of these events. The Cyrus Cylinder, now in the British Museum, is sometimes called the first declaration of human rights, although historians point out that it is also royal propaganda.

episodes.title: The Rock of Behistun
episodes.excerpt: Darius carves his story a hundred metres up a cliff, in three languages, and unlocks an ancient script for the modern world.
episodes.content:
In 522 BC, after the death of Cyrus's son Cambyses, a young noble named Darius seized the throne with six companions. Rebellions broke out across the empire, and Darius spent his first year fighting nineteen battles to crush them.

To tell his version of events, he had a huge inscription carved high on a cliff at Behistun, beside the road from Babylon to Ecbatana, in western Iran. It shows Darius standing over a defeated rival, with rebel kings roped together before him, and the text is written in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian.

More than two thousand years later, in the 1830s and 1840s, a British officer named Henry Rawlinson climbed the cliff on ladders and ropes to copy the text. Because the three versions said the same thing, scholars could use them to decipher cuneiform writing, opening up the lost history of Mesopotamia.

episodes.title: The King's Road
episodes.excerpt: Couriers on fresh horses carry the king's orders 2,500 kilometres across the empire in about a week.
episodes.content:
Darius divided his vast empire into provinces called satrapies, each ruled by a governor, the satrap, who collected taxes and kept order. To hold it all together he needed news to travel fast.

The most famous of his roads, the Royal Road, ran some 2,500 kilometres from Sardis in western Anatolia to Susa in Iran. The Greek historian Herodotus counted 111 stations along it, where fresh horses and riders waited. A traveller on foot needed about three months to cover it; the king's couriers, riding in relays, could do it in about a week.

Herodotus wrote that nothing mortal travelled faster than these messengers, and that neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness stopped them from completing their stage. Some two thousand years later those words were carved on the main post office in New York.

episodes.title: The Pass of Thermopylae
episodes.excerpt: 480 BC: Xerxes bridges the sea to invade Greece, and a few thousand Greeks hold a narrow pass.
episodes.content:
Darius's son Xerxes inherited both the empire and his father's unfinished war with the Greeks. In 480 BC he led one of the largest armies of the ancient world into Europe, crossing the Hellespont on two bridges made of ships lashed together.

At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, between the mountains and the sea, a Greek force of a few thousand men, led by King Leonidas of Sparta and his three hundred Spartans, blocked the road. For two days the Persians could not break through.

Then a local Greek named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain path that led behind the pass. Leonidas sent most of the Greeks away and stayed with his Spartans and a few allies, who fought until they were all killed. Xerxes marched on and burned Athens, but that September his fleet was defeated at Salamis, and the invasion of Greece failed.

episodes.title: Nomads from the East
episodes.excerpt: Driven from the borders of China, a nomad people travels thousands of kilometres and founds an empire.
episodes.content:
In the second century BC a nomadic people the Chinese called the Yuezhi lived on the grasslands of what is now Gansu in north-western China. Around 170 BC they were defeated by their powerful neighbours, the Xiongnu, and forced to move west.

After years of wandering they settled in Bactria, the land along the Oxus river in today's northern Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. A Chinese envoy, Zhang Qian, visited them there around 128 BC and reported that they had become rich and settled.

The Yuezhi were divided into five clans. In the first century AD the chief of one of them, the Kushans, a man named Kujula Kadphises, united the five under his rule. He crossed the Hindu Kush and took Gandhara, the region around Peshawar and Taxila. The Kushan Empire had begun.

episodes.title: Kanishka the Great
episodes.excerpt: A king at Peshawar whose coins honour Greek, Persian and Indian gods, and the Buddha.
episodes.content:
The greatest of the Kushan kings, Kanishka, came to the throne around AD 127. From his winter capital at Purushapura, today's Peshawar, he ruled lands stretching from Central Asia across Gandhara and deep into the plains of northern India.

In 1993 an inscription in the Bactrian language was found at Rabatak in northern Afghanistan. In it Kanishka lists his ancestors and the cities he ruled, and it has helped historians sort out the order of the Kushan kings.

His coins show how many worlds met in his empire. Alongside the standing king, they carry Greek gods like Helios, Iranian gods like Mithra, the Indian god Shiva, and, on a few rare coins, the Buddha himself. Buddhist tradition remembers Kanishka as a great patron who called a council of monks to settle their teachings.

episodes.title: The Great Stupa of Peshawar
episodes.excerpt: Chinese pilgrims called it the tallest tower they had ever seen. In 1908 an archaeologist found its relic casket.
episodes.content:
Outside Peshawar, Kanishka built an enormous Buddhist stupa topped by a tall wooden tower crowned with gilded parasols. Chinese pilgrims who walked thousands of kilometres to visit Gandhara wrote about it with awe. Faxian, who came around AD 400, called it the tallest of all the towers he had seen on his journey.

Over the centuries it was struck by lightning, rebuilt and finally ruined, until only a mound remained at a place called Shah-ji-ki-Dheri. In 1908 and 1909 the archaeologist D. B. Spooner excavated the mound and, deep in its foundations, found a casket of gilded metal.

On its lid sit the Buddha and two figures, and around its side runs a frieze with a king, probably Kanishka himself. An inscription names Kanishka. Inside were small fragments of bone, which were given to Buddhists in Burma and are kept in Mandalay. The casket itself is in the Peshawar Museum.

episodes.title: A Buddha in a Greek Robe
episodes.excerpt: In the workshops of Gandhara, sculptors give the Buddha a human face, with wavy hair and flowing folds.
episodes.content:
For centuries after his death the Buddha was not shown in human form in Indian art. He was represented by symbols instead: a footprint, an empty throne, a tree, a wheel. In the early centuries AD, in Gandhara and in Mathura in India, sculptors began to carve him as a man.

The Gandhara sculptors worked mostly in grey-blue schist. Their Buddha has wavy hair, a calm face and a heavy robe that falls in deep folds, much like a Greek or Roman statue. Gandhara had been ruled by Greek kings after Alexander, and it traded with the Roman world, and its artists blended those traditions with Indian ideas.

One of the most powerful works of Gandhara art is the Fasting Buddha, found at Sikri near Mardan in the nineteenth century. It shows the Buddha starved to skin and bone during his years of hardship before enlightenment. It is one of the treasures of the Lahore Museum.

episodes.title: The Silk Road Through Taxila
episodes.excerpt: Roman glass, Chinese lacquer and Indian ivory: the Kushans sit at the crossroads of the ancient world.
episodes.content:
The Kushan empire sat in the middle of the trade routes later called the Silk Road. Chinese silk travelled west through its lands, Indian spices and cotton went north and west, and Roman gold and glass came east. The Kushans struck gold coins on the Roman standard to make trade easier.

Taxila, near today's Islamabad, was one of the great cities on these roads. The Kushans built a new city there, Sirsukh, and the hills around it filled with monasteries such as Jaulian and Mohra Moradu, where monks studied and pilgrims stayed. Taxila became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.

At Begram in Afghanistan, once a Kushan summer capital, archaeologists in the 1930s opened two sealed rooms full of treasures: Roman glass and bronzes, Chinese lacquer boxes and carved Indian ivories, all side by side. In the third century AD the Sasanian Persians took the western Kushan lands, and the empire slowly broke apart.

posts.title: Why We Tell History Like a Drama Serial
posts.excerpt: Short episodes, cliffhangers and a release schedule: how Something Historic tells its stories.
posts.content:
Most of us remember the history we were taught at school as dates and names. Yet the same events, told as stories with people, choices and consequences, are as gripping as any drama on television.

That is why every story on this site is a series of short episodes. Each one takes a few minutes to read, ends at a turning point, and leads to the next. New episodes arrive on a schedule, so you can follow an empire the way you would follow a serial.

Every story is published in both English and Urdu, so you can read in the language you think in, or switch between them.

posts.title: Five Mughal Gardens You Can Still Walk In
posts.excerpt: From Kabul to Lahore to Kashmir, the paradise gardens the Mughals left behind.
posts.content:
Babur missed the gardens of Central Asia so much that one of the first things he did in India was lay one out. His descendants made the charbagh, a garden divided into four by water channels, a symbol of their rule.

You can still walk in many of them: Bagh-e Babur in Kabul, where the first emperor is buried; the Shalimar Gardens in Lahore, built by Shah Jahan; Nishat and Shalimar Bagh on the shores of Dal Lake in Srinagar; and the gardens around Humayun's Tomb in Delhi.

Go early in the morning, when the fountains run and the light is soft, and you will understand why the Mughals called these gardens a glimpse of paradise.

posts.title: The Coffeehouses of Istanbul
posts.excerpt: How a new drink created a new kind of public space, and worried a few sultans.
posts.content:
Coffee reached Istanbul from Yemen in the middle of the sixteenth century, and the first coffeehouses opened soon after. They quickly became the places where men met to talk, play backgammon, listen to storytellers and hear the news.

Not everyone was pleased. Some religious scholars argued about whether coffee was permitted, and more than one sultan closed the coffeehouses for fear they bred gossip and rebellion. Each time they reopened.

Within a century the habit had travelled to Venice, London and Paris, where coffeehouses played much the same role.

posts.title: How Roman Roads Lasted Two Thousand Years
posts.excerpt: Layers of stone, a curved surface and a lot of soldiers: the engineering behind "all roads lead to Rome".
posts.content:
At its height the Roman Empire was joined by more than 80,000 kilometres of paved roads. Many were built by soldiers, so that armies could march quickly to any frontier.

A typical road was built in layers: a deep trench filled with large stones, then gravel and sand, then tightly fitted paving slabs on top. The surface was curved so that rain ran off into ditches on either side.

Some of these roads, such as the Via Appia south of Rome, can still be walked on today, and many modern European highways follow routes first laid out by Roman surveyors.

posts.title: The Badshahi Mosque: Aurangzeb's Gift to Lahore
posts.excerpt: Built in just two years, it was for centuries one of the largest mosques in the world.
posts.content:
The Badshahi Mosque, the "Imperial Mosque", was built by the emperor Aurangzeb between 1671 and 1673, facing the Alamgiri Gate of the Lahore Fort. Its courtyard can hold tens of thousands of worshippers, and for three centuries it was among the largest mosques on earth.

It is made of red sandstone inlaid with white marble, with three marble domes and four tall minarets at the corners of the courtyard. The design follows the Jama Masjid of Delhi, built by Aurangzeb's father Shah Jahan, but on an even grander scale.

Under Sikh rule in the nineteenth century the mosque was used as a stable and a magazine, and the British later used it as a garrison. It was returned to the Muslims of Lahore in the 1850s and restored over the following century. The poet Muhammad Iqbal is buried in a small tomb just outside its steps.

posts.title: The Palace of Mirrors in Lahore Fort
posts.excerpt: Thousands of tiny mirrors, one candle, and a sky full of stars: the Sheesh Mahal.
posts.content:
The Lahore Fort was rebuilt in brick and stone by Akbar in the 1560s, and each emperor after him added his own palaces. The most dazzling is the Sheesh Mahal, the Palace of Mirrors, built in 1631 and 1632 for Shah Jahan.

Its walls and ceilings are covered with thousands of small pieces of convex mirror set in plaster, a technique called ayina-kari. It is said that a single candle lit inside makes the whole hall glitter like a night sky. It was built for the private use of the empress and the royal family.

Outside, along the north-west walls of the fort, runs the Picture Wall, decorated in the time of Jahangir and Shah Jahan with glazed tiles showing elephant fights, polo players, angels and dragons. The fort and the Shalimar Gardens became a UNESCO World Heritage Site together in 1981.

posts.title: Wazir Khan Mosque: The Most Colourful Building in Lahore
posts.excerpt: Every surface painted or tiled: the mosque a governor built inside the walled city.
posts.content:
Inside the old walled city of Lahore, a short walk from the Delhi Gate, stands the Wazir Khan Mosque. It was built between 1634 and 1641 by Hakim Ilmuddin Ansari, a physician who became governor of Lahore under Shah Jahan and was known by the title Wazir Khan.

What makes it famous is its decoration. Almost every surface, inside and out, is covered with kashi-kari, glazed tile mosaic in blue, yellow, green and orange, or with fresco paintings of flowers, vases and cypress trees. Calligraphy of Quranic verses and Persian poetry runs across the walls.

The mosque was built together with a row of shops whose rent paid for its upkeep, and it sat in the middle of a busy bazaar. A long restoration in the 2010s, led by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture and the Walled City of Lahore Authority, uncovered paintings hidden for generations under later layers.

posts.title: Small Paintings, Big Worlds: The Art of Mughal Miniatures
posts.excerpt: Persian masters, Indian painters and an emperor who could tell every artist's hand.
posts.content:
When the emperor Humayun returned to India from exile in Persia, he brought two Persian master painters with him, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad. Under his son Akbar they led a royal workshop in which more than a hundred painters, many of them Hindus from India, worked side by side.

Their first great project was the Hamzanama, the adventures of the hero Amir Hamza, painted on large sheets of cloth around 1562 to 1577. It had about 1,400 paintings, full of giants, dragons, battles and magic, and was shown to the emperor while storytellers read the text aloud.

Under Jahangir the style changed. He preferred single portraits and studies of nature, and his painter Ustad Mansur made exact pictures of birds, flowers and animals, including a zebra and a turkey brought to the court. Jahangir boasted that he could name the painter of any picture just by looking at it.

posts.title: The Long Journey of the Koh-i-Noor
posts.excerpt: Delhi, Kandahar, Lahore, London: the diamond that has had more owners than almost any object on earth.
posts.content:
No one knows exactly where the Koh-i-Noor was mined, though it almost certainly came from the riverbeds of the Deccan in southern India. The first clear description of it comes from the time of Nadir Shah, who carried it from Delhi to Persia in 1739, set in the Peacock Throne. Tradition says it was he who called it Koh-i-Noor, the "Mountain of Light".

After Nadir Shah was murdered, the stone passed to his Afghan general Ahmad Shah Durrani, founder of modern Afghanistan. In 1813 the exiled Afghan king Shah Shuja handed it over to Maharaja Ranjit Singh in Lahore, who wore it on his arm.

When the British annexed the Punjab in 1849, the treaty required the Koh-i-Noor to be surrendered to Queen Victoria. In 1852 it was recut in London, shrinking from about 186 carats to about 106. Today it is set in a crown in the Tower of London, and India, Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran have all claimed it.

posts.title: Ibn Battuta: The Traveller Who Became a Judge in Delhi
posts.excerpt: He left Tangier at twenty-one to make the pilgrimage, and came home twenty-four years later.
posts.content:
In 1325 a young man from Tangier in Morocco, Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Battuta, set out to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He did not return home for twenty-four years, and over his lifetime he travelled something like 120,000 kilometres, more than any known traveller before the age of steam.

In 1333 he crossed the Indus into the lands of Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq. The sultan was famously generous to learned foreigners and made him a qazi, a judge, in Delhi, where he stayed for about seven years. In 1342 the sultan sent him as an ambassador to China, a journey that ended in shipwreck and years of wandering through the Maldives, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

Back in Morocco, he dictated his memories to a scholar named Ibn Juzayy, who finished the book in 1355. Known as the Rihla, "The Journey", it is one of our richest sources for life in the fourteenth-century world, from the markets of Delhi to the courts of Mali.

posts.title: Amir Khusrau, the Parrot of India
posts.excerpt: Poet, musician and Sufi: the man whose verses are still sung at every qawwali.
posts.content:
Amir Khusrau was born in 1253 at Patiali, near the Ganges, to a Turkish father and an Indian mother. He served as a court poet to several sultans of Delhi, from the Slave dynasty to the Khaljis and Tughlaqs, and wrote a vast amount of Persian poetry and history. Admirers called him Tuti-e-Hind, the Parrot of India.

He also wrote in Hindavi, the everyday language of Delhi that would later grow into Urdu and Hindi, and his riddles and songs are still known by heart. He was the beloved disciple of the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya, and tradition credits him with shaping qawwali, the devotional music of the Sufi shrines.

Nizamuddin Auliya died in 1325, and Khusrau died a few months later. He was buried near his master in Delhi, and qawwals at the shrine still sing his verses, like "Chhap tilak sab chheeni re mose naina milaike", seven centuries after he wrote them.

posts.title: Makli: A City of the Dead on a Hill in Sindh
posts.excerpt: About ten square kilometres of tombs, built across four centuries outside Thatta.
posts.content:
On a long, low ridge outside the town of Thatta in Sindh lies Makli, one of the largest burial grounds in the world. Spread over about ten square kilometres, it holds hundreds of thousands of graves, from simple stones to great domed tombs of kings, queens, saints and generals.

Most of the monuments date from the fourteenth to the eighteenth centuries, when Thatta was a rich port city ruled first by the Samma dynasty, then by the Arghuns and Tarkhans, and finally by Mughal governors. Each period left its own style: carved yellow sandstone with Hindu and Gujarati motifs, bright blue glazed tiles, and Mughal brick domes.

The finest is the tomb of the Samma ruler Jam Nizamuddin II, who died in the early sixteenth century; its stone walls are carved like lace. Makli became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981, but salt, rain and neglect have damaged many tombs, and conservation work is ongoing.

posts.title: Rohtas Fort: The Fortress Built to Keep the Mughals Out
posts.excerpt: Sher Shah Suri's massive fort near Jhelum, with four kilometres of walls and twelve gates.
posts.content:
In 1540 the Afghan leader Sher Shah Suri defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun and drove him out of India. To stop Humayun from coming back through the north-west, and to control the local Gakhar tribes, Sher Shah ordered a great fortress built in the hills near Jhelum, beginning in 1541.

Rohtas Fort has walls about four kilometres long, with dozens of bastions and twelve gates; the Sohail Gate and the Kabuli Gate are among the most impressive. It was built for war rather than luxury, with stepped wells inside so it could survive a long siege.

Ironically, the fort never faced the siege it was built for. Sher Shah died in 1545, and when Humayun returned in 1555 the garrison gave up without a fight. Rohtas became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997 as one of the finest examples of early Muslim military architecture in South Asia.

posts.title: The Grand Trunk Road: Two Thousand Years on One Highway
posts.excerpt: From Bengal to Kabul, the road Sher Shah rebuilt, with a well and a shady tree for every traveller.
posts.content:
A great road across northern India existed in the time of the Mauryan emperors more than two thousand years ago. But the highway we call the Grand Trunk Road owes most to Sher Shah Suri, who in the 1540s rebuilt and extended it from Sonargaon in Bengal to the Indus and beyond, towards Kabul.

Sher Shah planted shade trees along it and built sarais, or roadside inns, at regular intervals, each with a well, a mosque and separate kitchens for Hindu and Muslim travellers. Horsemen stationed at the sarais carried the royal post. Kos minars, brick pillars marking the distance, were added by the Mughals, and some still stand.

The British rebuilt the road again in the nineteenth century and gave it its English name. Rudyard Kipling called it "a river of life" in his novel Kim. Today, as the N-5 in Pakistan and national highways in India and Bangladesh, it still carries millions of people every day.

posts.title: Hagia Sophia: Fifteen Centuries Under One Dome
posts.excerpt: Church, mosque, museum and mosque again: the building that has seen the whole history of Istanbul.
posts.content:
