The emperor Justinian built Hagia Sophia, the church of "Holy Wisdom", in Constantinople between 532 and 537. His architects, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, gave it a dome so wide and so light that, to people standing underneath, it seemed to hang from heaven on a golden chain.

For nearly a thousand years it was the greatest church in the Christian world. When Mehmed II conquered the city in 1453 he turned it into a mosque. Minarets were added, the mosaics were gradually plastered over, and huge round panels with the names of God, the Prophet and the first caliphs were hung inside in the nineteenth century.

In 1934 the Turkish Republic made it a museum, and restorers uncovered many of the Byzantine mosaics. In 2020 it became a mosque again, while remaining open to visitors. Few buildings anywhere have played so many roles for so long.

posts.title: Inside Topkapı Palace
posts.excerpt: Four courtyards, a harem of four hundred rooms, and the treasures of the sultans.
posts.content:
Soon after conquering Constantinople, Mehmed II began a new palace on the point of land where the Bosphorus meets the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara. Topkapı Palace was the home and the seat of government of the Ottoman sultans for almost four centuries, until they moved to the European-style Dolmabahçe Palace in 1856.

It is not one building but a series of courtyards, each more private than the last. The outer courts held the mint, the kitchens and the council chamber where the viziers met. The innermost areas held the sultan's private rooms and the Harem, a maze of hundreds of rooms where the royal family lived.

In 1924 the palace became a museum. Visitors can see the Spoonmaker's Diamond, the emerald-studded Topkapı Dagger, Chinese porcelain collected by the sultans, and the Chamber of Holy Relics, which holds objects revered as belonging to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.

posts.title: The Piri Reis Map: An Admiral's Picture of the New World
posts.excerpt: Drawn in 1513 on gazelle skin, it shows the coast of South America only twenty-one years after Columbus.
posts.content:
Piri Reis was an Ottoman sea captain who learned his trade sailing with his uncle, the famous corsair Kemal Reis. In 1513 in Gallipoli he drew a world map on gazelle-skin parchment, combining around twenty older maps, including, he wrote, one drawn by Columbus himself.

Only a fragment survives, about a third of the original. It shows the Atlantic coasts of Spain and West Africa and, on the other side of the ocean, the coast of Brazil and the islands of the Caribbean, decorated with ships, animals and notes in Ottoman Turkish.

The map was forgotten for four centuries until it was found in 1929 during work on Topkapı Palace being turned into a museum. Since Columbus's own map is lost, the Piri Reis map is one of the best clues to how he saw the lands he had reached. Piri Reis also wrote the Kitab-ı Bahriye, a famous book of sailing directions for the Mediterranean.

posts.title: How the Tulip Travelled from Istanbul to Amsterdam
posts.excerpt: A flower named after a turban, a Habsburg ambassador, and the first great financial bubble.
posts.content:
Long before the Netherlands became famous for tulips, they grew wild in Central Asia and were loved in the gardens of Persia and the Ottoman Empire. Ottoman poets compared them to beauty and devotion, and the flower appears again and again on Iznik tiles, carpets and textiles.

In the 1550s Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, the Habsburg ambassador to Suleiman the Magnificent, saw tulips in Turkish gardens and sent bulbs and seeds back to Vienna. The European word "tulip" probably comes from the Turkish word for turban, tülbend, perhaps because of the flower's shape. In 1593 the botanist Carolus Clusius planted tulips in the new botanical garden at Leiden in Holland.

The Dutch went wild for them. In the 1630s rare striped bulbs sold for more than the price of a house, until the market collapsed in February 1637. Back in Istanbul, the reign of Sultan Ahmed III from 1718 to 1730 became known as the Tulip Era, a time of garden parties, poetry and new fashions.

posts.title: The Janissaries and the World's Oldest Military Band
posts.excerpt: Elite infantry, cooking pots as symbols, and drums that made Europe tremble.
posts.content:
The Janissaries, from the Turkish yeniçeri, "new soldiers", were founded in the fourteenth century as the Ottoman sultan's personal infantry. For centuries they were recruited through the devshirme, trained from boyhood, paid regular salaries and forbidden to marry, so that their only family was the corps.

Their symbols came from the kitchen. Units were organised around the cooking pot, their officers had titles like "chief soup-maker", and overturning the great pots was the signal of a mutiny. Over time they grew powerful enough to depose sultans, and in 1826 Sultan Mahmud II destroyed the corps in a single day.

The Janissaries marched to the music of the mehter, a band of kettle drums, cymbals, horns and the shrill zurna. It is often called the oldest military band in the world, and its sound so impressed Europe that Mozart and Beethoven imitated it in "Turkish" marches. The mehter was revived in the twentieth century and still performs in Istanbul.

posts.title: The Colosseum: Fifty Thousand Seats and a Hundred Days of Games
posts.excerpt: Built on the site of Nero's private lake, it was Rome's gift to its people, and its most brutal stage.
posts.content:
After the suicide of the emperor Nero, the new emperor Vespasian drained the lake in Nero's private palace grounds and, around AD 70, began building a giant amphitheatre there, a gift to the people of Rome. His son Titus opened it in AD 80 with a hundred days of games.

The Flavian Amphitheatre, as it was officially called, could seat about fifty thousand spectators, arranged by social rank from the senators at the front to women and the poor at the top. Sailors from the navy worked a huge canvas awning, the velarium, to shade the crowd. Under the arena, a maze of tunnels and lifts let animals and fighters appear suddenly through trapdoors.

Gladiator fights continued into the fifth century and animal hunts into the sixth. Later, earthquakes brought down part of the outer wall, and for centuries its stones were carried off to build palaces and churches. It remains the largest amphitheatre ever built.

posts.title: The Pont du Gard: Water Across a Valley
posts.excerpt: Fifty kilometres of aqueduct, a drop of just twelve metres, and a bridge three tiers high.
posts.content:
In the first century AD the Roman city of Nemausus, today's Nîmes in southern France, needed more water. Engineers built an aqueduct to bring it from springs near Uzès. The channel was about fifty kilometres long, yet the total drop from beginning to end was only about twelve metres, a gradient so gentle it is still admired.

Where the aqueduct had to cross the valley of the river Gardon, the Romans built the Pont du Gard: three tiers of stone arches, nearly forty-nine metres high, made of blocks fitted together without mortar. The water channel ran along the very top.

The aqueduct carried millions of litres a day to the city's fountains, baths and houses. After it fell out of use the bridge survived because local people used its lower tier as a road bridge. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the best-preserved Roman structures in the world.

posts.title: Hadrian's Wall and a Birthday Invitation
posts.excerpt: The edge of the Roman world, and a letter from one officer's wife to another.
posts.content:
In AD 122 the emperor Hadrian visited Britain and ordered a wall built across the north of the island, from the river Tyne in the east to the Solway Firth in the west, about 117 kilometres. It had small forts every Roman mile, turrets between them, and larger forts along its length, and it marked the northern frontier of the empire.

The wall was not a sealed barrier but a controlled border, where people and goods could be watched and taxed. Soldiers from all over the empire served there, from Syria and North Africa to the Rhine.

At Vindolanda, a fort just south of the wall, archaeologists since 1973 have found hundreds of thin wooden writing tablets preserved in wet soil. One of them, written around AD 100, is an invitation from Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina to come to her birthday party. It contains what may be the oldest known writing in Latin by a woman.

posts.title: The Secret of Roman Concrete
posts.excerpt: Why harbour walls built two thousand years ago are still standing in the sea.
posts.content:
The Romans did not invent concrete, but they mastered it. Their key ingredient was volcanic ash from around the Bay of Naples, called pozzolana after the town of Pozzuoli. Mixed with lime and rubble, it set into a hard, durable stone, even underwater.

With concrete the Romans could build things no one had built before. The Pantheon in Rome, rebuilt under Hadrian in the 120s, has a dome forty-three metres across, and it is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

Scientists have recently found out why Roman concrete lasts so long. In harbour walls, seawater reacts with the volcanic ash to grow new minerals that strengthen the concrete over time. Other studies found small lumps of lime that can dissolve and seal cracks when water seeps in, so the concrete partly heals itself. Engineers today are studying these recipes for greener building materials.

posts.title: What Really Happened to the Library of Alexandria?
posts.excerpt: Not one great fire, but a slow fading over centuries.
posts.content:
Soon after Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in Egypt, the Greek kings who ruled after him, the Ptolemies, set out to collect all the knowledge of the world. In the early third century BC they founded the Museum, a research institute, and with it a great library.

The Ptolemies were said to search every ship that docked in Alexandria for books; the originals were copied and the owners were given the copies back. Scholars working there included Eratosthenes, who calculated the circumference of the earth with remarkable accuracy, and the editors who produced the standard texts of Homer.

The popular story says the library was destroyed in one terrible fire. In reality, Julius Caesar's fire in 48 BC damaged some books, royal funding faded under the Romans, and the institution declined over centuries of war and neglect. In 2002 Egypt opened the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, a great modern library, near the site of the ancient one.

posts.title: The Rosetta Stone: One Decree, Three Scripts
posts.excerpt: A broken slab found by French soldiers in 1799 let the world read hieroglyphs again.
posts.content:
In July 1799 French soldiers rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, in the Nile Delta, found a broken slab of dark stone covered in writing. It was a decree issued by Egyptian priests in 196 BC in honour of the young king Ptolemy V.

The decree was written three times: in hieroglyphs, the sacred picture-writing of temples; in Demotic, the everyday Egyptian script; and in ancient Greek, which scholars could still read. That made it a key to the lost language. When the French surrendered Egypt in 1801 the stone went to Britain, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

The English scholar Thomas Young made early progress, but it was the Frenchman Jean-François Champollion who cracked the system, announcing his discovery in 1822. He showed that hieroglyphs stood both for sounds and for ideas. After fourteen centuries of silence, the Egyptians could speak again.

posts.title: How the Ancient Egyptians Made a Mummy
posts.excerpt: Seventy days, a bed of salt, and a heart left in place for the final judgement.
posts.content:
The Egyptians believed that the body had to survive for the soul to live on in the afterlife. Over many centuries their embalmers developed a careful process that took about seventy days. The Greek historian Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the fifth century BC, described it in detail.

First the brain was removed, often through the nose with a hook, and thrown away. The organs of the abdomen were taken out through a cut in the side and preserved separately, often in four canopic jars. The heart, believed to be the seat of thought and feeling, was usually left in place, because it would be weighed against a feather in the judgement of the dead.

The body was then covered in natron, a natural salt, for about forty days to dry it out. Finally it was anointed with oils and resins and wrapped in hundreds of metres of linen bandages, with protective amulets placed between the layers. Today scientists study mummies with CT scanners and DNA analysis, without unwrapping them.

posts.title: Cleopatra Lived Closer to the Moon Landing Than to the Pyramids
posts.excerpt: A surprising fact about time, and what it tells us about how long ancient Egypt lasted.
posts.content:
Here is a fact that surprises almost everyone. The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC. Cleopatra VII, the last ruler of ancient Egypt, died in 30 BC. The first moon landing was in AD 1969. That means Cleopatra lived about 2,500 years after the pyramid was built, and only about 2,000 years before Neil Armstrong walked on the moon.

To Cleopatra, the pyramids were already ancient monuments, older to her than the Roman Republic is to us. Egyptian civilisation lasted so long that its own people visited and restored the ruins of their ancestors, and some pharaohs carried out what we would call archaeology.

Cleopatra herself was not ethnically Egyptian. She belonged to the Ptolemies, a Greek-speaking dynasty from Macedonia that had ruled Egypt for nearly three centuries. According to the writer Plutarch, she was the first of her family to learn the Egyptian language, and she spoke many others as well.

posts.title: The Temple That Was Moved Up a Hill
posts.excerpt: In the 1960s engineers cut Ramesses II's giant temple into blocks and rebuilt it out of reach of a new lake.
posts.content:
Around 1264 BC Ramesses II had two temples carved into a sandstone cliff at Abu Simbel in Nubia, far to the south of Egypt. The facade of the larger one has four seated statues of the king, each about twenty metres tall. Over time the sand covered it, and it was rediscovered by a Swiss traveller, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, in 1813.

In the 1960s Egypt began building the Aswan High Dam, whose lake would drown the temples for ever. UNESCO launched an international campaign to save them. Between 1964 and 1968 engineers cut the temples into more than a thousand huge blocks and rebuilt them about sixty-five metres higher and two hundred metres back from the river, inside an artificial hill.

The ancient builders had aligned the great temple so that twice a year, around 22 February and 22 October, the rising sun shines deep inside it and lights up the statues in the sanctuary. The engineers worked hard to preserve that effect, and it still happens, a day off from the original dates. The rescue inspired the creation of UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1972.

posts.title: Mehrgarh: Farming and Dentistry Nine Thousand Years Ago
posts.excerpt: At the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan lies one of the oldest farming villages in South Asia.
posts.content:
In 1974 a French team led by the archaeologist Jean-François Jarrige began excavating a site called Mehrgarh, on the Kachhi plain near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan. They found a village that had been lived in from around 7000 BC, thousands of years before the cities of the Indus.

The people of early Mehrgarh grew barley and wheat, kept cattle, sheep and goats, and lived in houses of mud brick. They buried their dead with beads of shell and turquoise from distant places, showing that trade routes existed even then. Over thousands of years the village grew, and its potters and craftsmen became highly skilled.

In 2006 scientists announced an astonishing find: several teeth from Mehrgarh burials, between about 7,500 and 9,000 years old, had small holes drilled into them with a bow drill, probably by people who had worked out how to treat toothache. It is the oldest evidence of dentistry in the world. Mehrgarh shows that the Indus civilisation grew from very deep local roots.

posts.title: Fair Weights: How the Indus Cities Measured the World
posts.excerpt: Cubes of polished stone in a system so exact it was used for seven centuries.
posts.content:
Across the Indus cities, from Harappa to Mohenjo-daro to Lothal, archaeologists have found small cubes of polished stone, usually chert. They are weights, and they follow the same standard everywhere, over a vast area and for hundreds of years.

The smaller weights double each time, in the ratio 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, and the larger ones follow a decimal pattern. The most common weight, at about 13.7 grams, was the "16" unit. Merchants could weigh anything from beads to grain using the same set, and a trader in one city could trust a weight from another.

The Indus people measured length carefully too. A broken scale of shell from Mohenjo-daro and one of ivory from Lothal are marked with fine, evenly spaced lines. Their bricks were also made in standard proportions, usually 1:2:4. Such uniformity suggests a society with strong shared rules, even though we do not know who made them.

posts.title: Lothal: A Harbour Town of the Indus Civilisation
posts.excerpt: A great brick basin in Gujarat that may be one of the oldest docks in the world.
posts.content:
Lothal lies in Gujarat, in western India, near the head of the Gulf of Khambhat. It was excavated between 1955 and 1960 by the Indian archaeologist S. R. Rao, who found a small but busy town of the Indus civilisation, dating from around 2400 BC.

Its most striking feature is a large rectangular basin, about 220 metres long, lined with baked bricks. Rao believed it was a dockyard, where boats could come in from the sea at high tide. Some scholars think it may have been a reservoir instead, and the debate continues.

What is certain is that Lothal was a centre of craft and trade. It had a bead factory where workers drilled carnelian and agate, a warehouse with clay sealings from goods packed for shipping, and finds that link it to the Persian Gulf. A visit to its small site museum shows how far the reach of the Indus cities extended.

posts.title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Science of Light
posts.excerpt: A scholar under house arrest in Cairo works out how we really see.
posts.content:
Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra around 965 and later moved to Cairo. According to a famous story, he boasted that he could control the floods of the Nile, failed, and pretended to be mad to escape the anger of the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, spending years confined to his house.

Whatever the truth of the story, he used his time well. In his Book of Optics, written in the early eleventh century, he argued that we see because light travels from objects into our eyes, not because our eyes send out rays, as many Greek thinkers had believed.

What made him special was his method. He tested his ideas with careful experiments, including a dark room with a tiny hole that projected an upside-down image of the outside world, the camera obscura. Translated into Latin, his book influenced European scientists for centuries, and many historians count him among the founders of the experimental method.

posts.title: Al-Biruni Measures the Earth from a Fort in the Salt Range
posts.excerpt: A thousand years ago, at Nandana near Jhelum, a scholar worked out the size of the planet using one mountain.
posts.content:
Abu Rayhan al-Biruni was born in Khwarazm in 973 and became one of the greatest scholars of his age, writing on astronomy, mathematics, geography and history. In the early eleventh century he came to India with the armies of Mahmud of Ghazni.

At the hill fort of Nandana in the Salt Range, near Pind Dadan Khan in today's Jhelum district, he used a new method to measure the earth. He first measured the height of a hill, then climbed it and measured how far the horizon dipped below the horizontal. With these two numbers and trigonometry he calculated the radius of the earth.

His answer was close to the modern value of about 6,371 kilometres, an astonishing achievement with simple instruments. Al-Biruni also learned Sanskrit and wrote Kitab al-Hind, a careful and respectful study of Indian science, religion and customs. The ruins of Nandana fort can still be visited today.

posts.title: How Paper Travelled from China to Baghdad
posts.excerpt: A battle in Central Asia, a famous legend, and the mills that changed the world of books.
posts.content:
Paper was invented in China, and for centuries the secret of making it from plant fibres stayed in East Asia. A famous story says it reached the Islamic world in 751, after the Battle of Talas in Central Asia, when Chinese prisoners taken by the Abbasid army taught papermaking in Samarkand.

Historians now think the story is too neat, since paper was probably already known in Central Asia before then. But it is certain that Samarkand became famous for its paper, and that by the 790s, in the time of Harun al-Rashid, paper was being made in Baghdad itself.

Paper was cheaper than parchment and harder to alter than papyrus, so government offices adopted it quickly. Booksellers' markets grew, libraries filled, and the translation movement of the House of Wisdom could spread its books widely. From Baghdad the craft travelled to Damascus, Cairo and Morocco, and reached Europe through Muslim Spain.

posts.title: The Thousand and One Nights: Where Did Aladdin Come From?
posts.excerpt: Persian roots, Baghdad settings, and two famous stories added in eighteenth-century Paris.
posts.content:
The frame story is famous: a king, betrayed by his wife, marries a new bride each night and has her killed in the morning, until the clever Shahrazad begins telling him stories and stops each one at the most exciting moment. The collection grew from a Persian book called Hazar Afsan, "A Thousand Tales", translated into Arabic by the ninth century.

Over the following centuries storytellers in Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo added new tales, and many are set in the Baghdad of Harun al-Rashid, who wanders the streets in disguise with his vizier Ja'far. The oldest surviving fragment of the Arabic text, a single page, dates from the ninth century.

Between 1704 and 1717 the Frenchman Antoine Galland translated the Nights into French, and Europe fell in love with them. Galland's version included "Aladdin" and "Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves", which are not found in any older Arabic manuscript. He heard them from Hanna Diyab, a young Syrian storyteller from Aleppo who visited Paris in 1709.

posts.title: Fatima al-Fihri and the Oldest University in the World
posts.excerpt: In 859 a merchant's daughter in Fez used her inheritance to build a mosque, and it became a centre of learning that still runs today.
posts.content:
Fatima al-Fihri was born in Kairouan, in today's Tunisia, and moved with her family to the city of Fez in Morocco. Her father was a successful merchant, and when he died she and her sister Maryam inherited his fortune.

In 859 Fatima used her share to found a mosque in her neighbourhood, al-Qarawiyyin, named after the people of Kairouan. Over the next centuries it grew into a great centre of teaching, attracting students in law, theology, grammar, astronomy and medicine from across North Africa and al-Andalus.

UNESCO and the Guinness World Records describe al-Qarawiyyin as the oldest existing, continually operating educational institution in the world. Its library, restored and reopened in 2016, holds precious manuscripts, including one of the oldest copies of the Muqaddimah of Ibn Khaldun. A woman's gift became one of the oldest universities on earth.

posts.title: The Alhambra: The Red Palace of Granada
posts.excerpt: Water, light and poetry carved in plaster: the last great palace of al-Andalus.
posts.content:
The Alhambra, from the Arabic al-Qal'a al-Hamra, "the Red Fortress", stands on a hill above Granada. The Nasrid sultans, who ruled the last Muslim kingdom in Spain from 1238 to 1492, turned an older fortress into a city of palaces, gardens and baths.

Most of what visitors admire today was built in the fourteenth century under Yusuf I and Muhammad V. The Court of the Lions has a fountain held up by twelve marble lions, with channels of water running to the four sides. Walls and ceilings are covered with carved plaster, coloured tiles and honeycomb-like domes called muqarnas.

Everywhere the walls speak. Poems by the court poet Ibn Zamrak are carved into the rooms they describe, and one phrase is repeated thousands of times: "wa la ghaliba illa Allah", "There is no victor but God". After 1492 the palace was neglected until the American writer Washington Irving lived there and published his Tales of the Alhambra in 1832, making it famous again.

posts.title: Ziryab, the Blackbird Who Taught Córdoba Style
posts.excerpt: A musician from Baghdad who added a string to the oud, and changed how Andalusians dined and dressed.
posts.content:
Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn Nafi was a gifted singer from the court of Baghdad, nicknamed Ziryab, "the blackbird", for his dark complexion and beautiful voice. According to later historians, his talent made his teacher jealous, and he left Baghdad to seek his fortune in the west.

In 822 he arrived in Córdoba, where the emir Abd al-Rahman II welcomed him with a generous salary. He founded a school of music and is said to have added a fifth string to the oud, the lute that later gave Europe its own word "lute".

Ziryab became the arbiter of fashion in al-Andalus. Tradition credits him with introducing a meal served in courses, from soup to dessert, glass cups instead of metal, new hairstyles, a kind of toothpaste, and different clothes for each season. Some of these stories may be exaggerated, but they show how Baghdad's culture flowed into Spain, and from there into Europe.

posts.title: Abbas ibn Firnas: The Man Who Tried to Fly a Thousand Years Ago
posts.excerpt: Córdoba, ninth century: an inventor covers himself in feathers and leaps from a hill.
posts.content:
Abbas ibn Firnas was a scholar, poet and inventor at the court of Córdoba in the ninth century. He is credited with a method for cutting rock crystal, a water clock, and a planetarium-like room where he could show the stars, clouds, thunder and lightning.

He is most remembered for an attempt to fly. The seventeenth-century historian al-Maqqari, quoting an earlier poet, writes that ibn Firnas covered himself in feathers, attached a pair of wings, and launched himself from a height. He glided for some distance before landing badly and injuring his back. Al-Maqqari says he had forgotten that birds use their tails to land.

We cannot be sure how far he flew, since the account was written centuries later. But ibn Firnas has become a hero of aviation history. A crater on the moon is named after him, as is a bridge in Córdoba, and his statue stands near Baghdad's airport.

posts.title: Marco Polo at the Court of Kublai Khan
posts.excerpt: A Venetian merchant's son spends seventeen years in China, then tells his story in a prison cell.
posts.content:
In 1271 seventeen-year-old Marco Polo left Venice with his father and uncle, merchants who had already visited the Mongol court. Travelling overland through Persia and Central Asia, they reached the summer palace of Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis, around 1275.

Marco stayed in China for about seventeen years and, by his own account, served the khan on missions across the empire. He described paper money, coal burned as fuel, the great canal, the postal system and the vast city the Mongols called Khanbaliq, today's Beijing. The Mongol peace, which kept the roads across Asia safe for traders, made such a journey possible.

In 1295 the Polos returned to Venice. A few years later Marco was captured in a war with Genoa, and in prison he told his story to a writer of romances, Rustichello of Pisa, who wrote it down. Some scholars have doubted parts of it, but many of its details have been confirmed by Chinese and Persian sources.

posts.title: The Yam: The Mongol Empire's Pony Express
posts.excerpt: Relay stations across Asia, and a metal pass that opened every door.
posts.content:
Ruling an empire that stretched from Korea to Hungary needed fast communication. The Mongols built a network of relay stations called the yam, expanded greatly under Genghis Khan's son Ögedei in the 1230s. Stations stood roughly a day's ride apart, sometimes closer, stocked with fresh horses, food and shelter.

Official riders carried a paiza, a tablet of wood, silver or gold engraved with the khan's command, which entitled them to horses and supplies at every station. In an emergency messengers could ride day and night, changing horses at each stop, and cover hundreds of kilometres in a day.

Marco Polo was amazed by the system and claimed there were tens of thousands of horses waiting at the stations of China alone. The yam carried not only orders but also envoys, merchants and news, helping to knit the vast Mongol world together.

posts.title: The Silver Tree of Karakorum
posts.excerpt: A French goldsmith, a Mongol khan, and a fountain that poured four drinks at once.
posts.content:
Karakorum, in the valley of the Orkhon River in central Mongolia, became the capital of the Mongol Empire under Ögedei, who built walls and a palace there in the 1230s. Merchants, craftsmen and envoys from all over the world lived in its quarters.

In 1254 a Flemish friar, William of Rubruck, visited the court of the Great Khan Möngke. In his report he described a wonder at the entrance to the palace: a great tree made of silver, with four silver lions at its roots and serpents winding up the trunk.

It had been made by Guillaume Boucher, a goldsmith from Paris who had been captured in Hungary and taken to Mongolia. At a signal from an angel figure with a trumpet at the top, servants hidden inside pumped drinks through the tree, and from the serpents' mouths flowed wine, mare's milk, rice wine and mead. Karakorum was later destroyed, and only ruins and a stone turtle remain today.

posts.title: Persepolis: The Gate of All Nations
posts.excerpt: Carved delegations, a giant terrace, and thirty thousand clay tablets that record workers' wages.
posts.content:
Persepolis stands on a huge stone terrace at the foot of a mountain in the province of Fars in southern Iran. Visitors entered by a grand double staircase, shallow enough to climb on horseback, and passed through the Gate of All Nations, guarded by giant winged bulls with human heads.

The reliefs on the staircases of the Apadana show twenty-three delegations from across the empire, each in its own dress, bringing gifts: Indians with gold dust, Arabs with a camel, Ethiopians with an elephant tusk, Lydians with fine vessels. Together they form a portrait of the whole empire.

In the 1930s archaeologists found tens of thousands of clay tablets in the fortification wall. They record the payment of rations of grain, wine and beer to the workers who built and ran the city, men and women alike, including extra rations for women who had just given birth. Persepolis became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

posts.title: Qanats: The Underground Rivers of Persia
posts.excerpt: Tunnels dug by hand three thousand years ago that still bring water to the desert.
posts.content:
In the dry plateau of Iran, rain is rare but water lies deep under the mountains. Nearly three thousand years ago the Persians found a way to reach it: the qanat, a gently sloping tunnel that carries groundwater from the foot of the hills to the fields and villages, using only gravity.

Diggers began with a "mother well" near the mountains, sometimes more than a hundred metres deep, then dug a tunnel back towards the surface, with vertical shafts every few dozen metres for air and to remove the earth. From above, a qanat looks like a line of craters across the desert.

Because the water flows underground, little is lost to evaporation. The technique spread to Afghanistan, Oman, North Africa and Spain, and in Balochistan in Pakistan the same tunnels are called karez. In 2016 UNESCO listed eleven Persian qanats as World Heritage, including the qanat of Gonabad, said to be about 2,700 years old and still flowing.

posts.title: Takht-i-Bahi: The Monastery on the Hill
posts.excerpt: Above the plains of Mardan, a Buddhist monastery that survived because it was hard to reach.
posts.content:
On a rocky hill about fifteen kilometres from Mardan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa stand the ruins of Takht-i-Bahi, one of the best-preserved Buddhist monasteries in Gandhara. Its name is often explained as "throne of the spring", after a spring on the hilltop.

The monastery was founded in the first century AD and expanded under the Kushans. Visitors can still walk through its courtyard of stupas surrounded by niches that once held statues, the monks' cells, the assembly hall and the underground meditation chambers. An inscription found here in the nineteenth century names the Indo-Parthian king Gondophares.

Because it stood high on a hill, the monastery escaped much of the destruction that hit sites on the plains, and it was used until about the seventh century. Takht-i-Bahi and the nearby walled town of Sahr-i-Bahlol became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.

posts.title: What Was the Silk Road, Really?
posts.excerpt: Not one road, not only silk, and the name is only 150 years old.
posts.content:
The phrase "Silk Road" was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen. People in the ancient world never used it. What it describes is not one road but a web of routes, by land and sea, that linked China with Central Asia, India, Persia, the Middle East and the Mediterranean.

Silk was only one of the goods that moved along it. Horses, glass, spices, cotton, paper, porcelain, gems and silver travelled too, and so did ideas: Buddhism spread from India and Gandhara to China along these routes, and later Islam spread east along them. Very few traders travelled the whole way; goods passed from hand to hand, city to city.

Pakistan sits at one of its great crossroads. Routes through the Khyber Pass, Taxila and Gilgit-Baltistan carried pilgrims and merchants for centuries. In the Karakoram, rock carvings along the old route near Chilas and Hunza record the names and prayers of travellers in many scripts, and today the Karakoram Highway follows parts of the same ancient path.

posts.title: Faxian and Xuanzang: Chinese Pilgrims in Gandhara
posts.excerpt: Two monks walked from China to Pakistan in search of the Buddha's teachings, and wrote down everything they saw.
posts.content:
Around AD 400 a Chinese monk named Faxian set out from Chang'an to find complete copies of the Buddhist monastic rules. He crossed the deserts of Central Asia and the mountains of the Karakoram, and travelled through Swat, Gandhara and Taxila before going on to the Ganges plain. He returned to China by sea more than a decade later.

Two centuries later, in 629, another monk, Xuanzang, left China without the emperor's permission and made an even longer journey. He studied at the great monastery of Nalanda in India and came home in 645 with hundreds of texts. He described Gandhara as a land of many ruined monasteries, past its golden age.

Their travel accounts are priceless to historians and archaeologists, who have used them to find and identify sites like the stupa of Kanishka at Peshawar. Xuanzang's journey also inspired the famous Chinese novel Journey to the West, with its monkey king companion.

posts.title: Swat: The Garden of Udyana
posts.excerpt: A green valley that was once a holy land of Buddhism, and the Buddha carved in its rock.
posts.content:
Long before it was famous for its mountains and rivers, the Swat valley was known as Udyana, "the garden", one of the holiest lands of Buddhism. Chinese pilgrims wrote of hundreds of monasteries along the Swat river, and the valley is linked by tradition with the teacher Padmasambhava, who later carried Buddhism to Tibet.

Since 1956 an Italian archaeological mission, begun by Giuseppe Tucci and Domenico Faccenna, has excavated sites such as Butkara I, a great stupa near Mingora that was rebuilt and enlarged several times over many centuries. Thousands of sculptures from Swat are displayed in the Swat Museum in Saidu Sharif.

Near the village of Jahanabad, a large seated Buddha carved into a rock face around the seventh century was badly damaged by militants in 2007. Italian and Pakistani experts restored its face between 2012 and 2016. Today it is again a symbol of Swat's long and peaceful history.

posts.title: A Visit to the Taxila Museum
posts.excerpt: Coins, jewellery, Buddhas and everyday objects from three ancient cities, in one quiet building.
posts.content:
The Taxila Museum stands near the ruins it was built to explain, about thirty-five kilometres from Islamabad. Its foundation stone was laid in 1918, during the excavations led by Sir John Marshall, and it opened to the public in 1928.

Its collections come from the three ancient cities of Taxila, Bhir Mound, Sirkap and Sirsukh, and from the monasteries around them, such as Jaulian and Dharmarajika. There are stucco and stone Buddhas, gold jewellery, silver cups, coins of Greek, Scythian, Parthian and Kushan kings, and ordinary things like toys, cooking pots and tools.

After the museum, visitors can walk the straight main street of Sirkap, laid out by Greek rulers in the second century BC, and climb to the monastery at Jaulian, where the stupas still carry rows of small seated Buddhas. Together they make one of the best days out in Pakistan for anyone who loves history.

posts.title: How Do Historians Know What Happened?
posts.excerpt: Chronicles, coins, inscriptions and rubbish heaps: the evidence behind every story we tell.
posts.content:
Every episode on Something Historic rests on evidence, and it helps to know what kinds there are. Historians divide sources into primary ones, made at the time, and secondary ones, written later by people studying the past. A letter by a Mughal emperor is primary; a modern biography of him is secondary.

Written sources include chronicles, memoirs such as the Baburnama, letters, laws and travel accounts. But writers had their own aims: court historians praised their masters, and enemies exaggerated crimes. So historians compare sources, ask who wrote each one and why, and look for evidence that was never meant to persuade anyone.

That is where archaeology helps. Coins show who ruled where and when, inscriptions record official claims, and even rubbish heaps reveal what people ate. Scientific methods like radiocarbon dating and DNA analysis add more. When we say "a legend says" in our stories, it means the evidence is weak, and we want you to know it.

posts.title: Hijri, AD and BC: How We Number the Years
posts.excerpt: Why there is no year zero, why the Islamic year moves through the seasons, and the eleven days Britain lost.
posts.content:
The Islamic calendar counts years from the Hijrah, the Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in AD 622, peace be upon him. It was adopted by the caliph Umar around 638. Its months follow the moon, so a Hijri year has about 354 days, eleven fewer than a solar year. That is why Ramadan moves through the seasons, coming about eleven days earlier each year.

The Christian era, counting from the traditional year of the birth of Jesus, was devised by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus in AD 525. Counting years before it as "BC" became common later, helped by the English scholar Bede in the eighth century. There is no year zero: 1 BC is followed directly by AD 1. Many historians now write BCE and CE instead.

In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII reformed the solar calendar to fix a drift in the date of Easter, and ten days were skipped. Protestant Britain waited until 1752, by which time eleven days had to be dropped: in that year, 2 September was followed by 14 September. Pakistan, like most of the world, uses both the Gregorian and the Hijri calendars every day.

posts.title: Saving Mohenjo-daro
posts.excerpt: Four and a half thousand years old, the city now faces salt, water and the weather.
posts.content:
When Mohenjo-daro was excavated in the 1920s, its bricks had been protected by earth for thousands of years. Once exposed to the air, they began to decay. The biggest enemy is salt: groundwater rises through the bricks, evaporates in the heat and leaves salt crystals that crumble them from inside.

In the 1970s UNESCO and Pakistan launched an international campaign to save the site, lowering the water table with tube wells and building embankments against the Indus, which had shifted dangerously close. The campaign ran until 1997. Since then, much of the city has been left unexcavated on purpose, because buried bricks are safer than exposed ones.

Heavy rains during the floods of 2022 damaged walls and drains, and conservation teams continue to work with traditional mud mortar and new methods. Archaeologists still have much to learn, because only about a third of the city has been dug. The best way to protect it is to visit with respect: don't climb on walls or take bricks home.

posts.title: The Khyber Pass: Gateway of Empires
posts.excerpt: Fifty-odd kilometres of mountain road that armies, traders and pilgrims have crossed for thousands of years.
posts.content:
The Khyber Pass winds for roughly fifty kilometres through the Spin Ghar mountains, linking the Peshawar valley with the Afghan side of the border at Torkham. For thousands of years it has been one of the main gateways between Central Asia and the plains of South Asia.

Persians, Greeks, Kushans, Huns, the armies of Mahmud of Ghazni and Babur all came through the passes of this frontier, and so did merchants with caravans of horses and fruit, and pilgrims heading for the monasteries of Gandhara. In 1836 the Sikh general Hari Singh Nalwa built Jamrud Fort at the eastern mouth of the pass.

The British fought three Anglo-Afghan wars along this route and built the Khyber railway, finished in 1925, with dozens of tunnels and bridges climbing to Landi Kotal. At Jamrud stands the Bab-e-Khyber, the gateway arch built in 1963, which has become a symbol of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

posts.title: Derawar Fort: Forty Bastions in the Cholistan Desert
posts.excerpt: A massive fort rising out of the sand south of Bahawalpur, visible from kilometres away.
posts.content:
Deep in the Cholistan desert, more than a hundred kilometres south of Bahawalpur, the walls of Derawar Fort rise suddenly out of the sand. Its forty great bastions, each about thirty metres high, can be seen from far across the dunes.

Tradition says the first fort here was built in the ninth century by a Rajput prince of the Bhati clan. In 1733 it was captured by Nawab Sadiq Muhammad Khan I of the Abbasi family, the rulers of Bahawalpur, and largely rebuilt in its present form. The nawabs used it as a stronghold, and the royal family's graves lie nearby.

Beside the fort stands a white marble mosque built in the nineteenth century, modelled on the Moti Masjid in the Red Fort of Delhi. Every year Derawar hosts the Cholistan Jeep Rally, which brings thousands of visitors to the desert. The fort itself needs urgent repair, and parts of its walls have collapsed in recent decades.

museums.title: Lahore Museum
museums.excerpt: Five thousand years of South Asia under one red-brick roof.
museums.content:
Founded in 1865 and moved in 1894 into the Mughal-Gothic building on The Mall designed by Sir Ganga Ram, the Lahore Museum is the oldest and one of the largest museums in Pakistan. Rudyard Kipling's father, John Lockwood Kipling, was one of its early curators, and the museum appears in the opening pages of the novel Kim.

Its galleries move from the Indus Valley and Gandhara through the Mughal and Sikh courts to the colonial era and the Pakistan Movement. The Gandhara collection is the jewel: few places on earth show so clearly how Greek, Persian and Indian art met along the old Silk Road.

museums.title: National Museum of Pakistan
museums.excerpt: The nation's story, from the Indus to independence.
museums.content:
Opened in 1950 in Frere Hall and moved in 1970 to its present building in Burns Garden, the National Museum of Pakistan holds the country's national collection. Its galleries trace the land from the Stone Age through the Indus civilization, Gandhara and the Islamic period to the creation of Pakistan.

The Quran gallery holds hundreds of manuscripts, some of them centuries old, and the independence gallery tells the story of 1947 through documents and photographs.

museums.title: Taxila Museum
museums.excerpt: Where Alexander's Greeks met the monks of Gandhara.
museums.content:
The foundation stone was laid in 1918 and the museum opened in 1928 to house finds from the excavations of Sir John Marshall at Taxila, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Taxila was a great city of learning for over a thousand years and was visited by Alexander the Great in 326 BC.

The collection comes from the three ancient cities of Bhir Mound, Sirkap and Sirsukh and from Buddhist monasteries such as Dharmarajika and Jaulian, so you can see the objects and then walk to the places they were found.

museums.title: Peshawar Museum
museums.excerpt: The life of the Buddha, told in Gandhara stone.
museums.content:
The museum began in 1907 in the Victoria Memorial Hall, a building that mixes British, Hindu, Buddhist and Islamic styles. Peshawar was the capital of the Kushan king Kanishka, and the museum holds one of the largest collections of Gandhara art in the world.

Its relief panels tell the Buddha's life story scene by scene, from his birth to his death, and other galleries show the arms, crafts and clothing of the peoples of the frontier.

Standing Buddhas and Bodhisattvas from Takht-i-Bahi and Sahri-Bahlol
Ethnographic galleries of the frontier tribes
The Victoria Memorial Hall building itself

museums.title: Mohenjo-daro Museum
museums.excerpt: A planned city, 4,500 years old, on the banks of the Indus.
museums.content:
Mohenjo-daro was one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilization, built around 2500 BC with straight streets, brick houses, covered drains and the famous Great Bath. It was rediscovered in the 1920s and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The site museum shows what the excavations found: seals carved with animals and a script no one has yet deciphered, toys, weights, beads and pottery. Many of the best-known finds are now in Karachi and New Delhi, but nothing replaces walking the city itself.

meta.tagline: A planned city, 4,500 years old, on the banks of the Indus.
meta.address: At the Mohenjo-daro archaeological site, Larkana District, Sindh
meta.hours: Open daily. Visit early in summer, when the site gets very hot.
meta.tickets: Entry fee covers the site; separate rate for foreign visitors.
highlights: Indus seals with the still-undeciphered script
Terracotta toys, weights and pottery
The Great Bath and the Buddhist stupa on the citadel
Streets and drains of a 4,500-year-old planned city

museums.title: Harappa Museum
museums.excerpt: The town that gave a whole civilization its name.
museums.content:
Harappa was the first Indus city to be excavated, in the 1920s, which is why the whole Indus civilization is often called the Harappan civilization. The site museum was set up in 1926 beside the mounds.

Its cases hold seals, beads, bangles, figurines and painted pottery, and a walk around the site takes you past granaries, workshops and the cemetery of a city that flourished more than 4,000 years ago.

meta.tagline: The town that gave a whole civilization its name.
meta.address: At the Harappa archaeological site, Sahiwal District, Punjab
meta.hours: Open daily. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee; separate rate for foreign visitors.
highlights: Carnelian and steatite beads from Harappan workshops
Painted pottery and terracotta figurines
Seals and weights used by Harappan traders
The granary and cemetery areas of the site

museums.title: Lahore Fort (Shahi Qila)
museums.excerpt: Akbar's citadel, Shah Jahan's Palace of Mirrors.
museums.content:
The fort was rebuilt in brick by the Mughal emperor Akbar from 1566, and every emperor after him added to it. Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb built halls, gardens and gateways, and the Sikh ruler Ranjit Singh later lived here. Together with the Shalamar Gardens it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Inside are the Sheesh Mahal, a hall covered in thousands of tiny mirrors, the marble Naulakha pavilion, and the Picture Wall, one of the longest tile murals in the world. Galleries in the fort show Mughal and Sikh arms, coins and paintings.

meta.tagline: Akbar's citadel, Shah Jahan's Palace of Mirrors.
meta.address: Walled City, next to the Badshahi Mosque, Lahore
meta.hours: Open daily. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Entry ticket; separate rate for foreign visitors. Some galleries are ticketed separately.
highlights: The Sheesh Mahal (Palace of Mirrors) built for Shah Jahan
The Picture Wall, decorated with tile and fresco scenes
The Naulakha pavilion and the Alamgiri Gate
Sikh-period gallery and the Mughal armoury

museums.title: Lok Virsa Heritage Museum
museums.excerpt: Pakistan's living crafts, music and costume in one place.
museums.content:
Lok Virsa, the National Institute of Folk and Traditional Heritage, was set up in 1974 to collect and protect the folk culture of Pakistan. Its Heritage Museum on the Shakarparian hills is one of the largest museums of living culture in the region.

Life-size scenes show the homes, clothes, crafts, music and festivals of every province, from Kalash dancers to Sindhi ajrak printers. The grounds host craft fairs and folk festivals through the year.

meta.tagline: Pakistan's living crafts, music and costume in one place.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: Galleries for each province, with life-size figures
Musical instruments, embroidery and woodwork
Truck art and folk painting
Seasonal folk festivals in the grounds

museums.title: Pakistan Monument Museum
museums.excerpt: The road to 1947, beneath four granite petals.
museums.content:
The museum opened in 2010 next to the Pakistan Monument, whose four large petals stand for the provinces and three smaller ones for the territories. It tells the story of the Pakistan Movement from the war of 1857 to independence in 1947.

Wax figures, dioramas and recreated rooms bring key moments to life, including the Lahore Resolution of 1940 and the leaders who shaped the new country.

meta.tagline: The road to 1947, beneath four granite petals.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: Wax figures of the leaders of the Pakistan Movement
Dioramas of the 1940 Lahore Resolution
Views over Islamabad from the monument
Murals inside the petals of the monument

museums.title: Allama Iqbal Museum (Javed Manzil)
museums.excerpt: The house where the poet of the East spent his last years.
museums.content:
Allama Muhammad Iqbal built Javed Manzil and named it after his son Javed. He lived here from 1935 until his death on 21 April 1938. The government later bought the house and turned it into a museum.

The rooms keep his furniture, clothes, books, letters and manuscripts, along with photographs and awards. It is a quiet, personal place to meet the poet behind the idea of Pakistan.

meta.tagline: The house where the poet of the East spent his last years.
meta.address: Allama Iqbal Road, near Lahore Railway Station, Lahore
meta.hours: Open most days; closed on some public holidays. Check before you go.
meta.tickets: Free or a small fee.
highlights: Iqbal's study, bedroom and personal belongings
Handwritten manuscripts and letters
His library of books in several languages
Medals, degrees and photographs

museums.title: Quaid-e-Azam House Museum (Flagstaff House)
museums.excerpt: Jinnah's Karachi home, kept as he left it.
museums.content:
Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah bought this colonial-era house, known as Flagstaff House, in 1943. After his death his sister Fatima Jinnah lived here until 1964. The house was later restored and opened as a museum.

The rooms show the furniture, clothes and personal things of the Quaid and Miss Fatima Jinnah, set out much as they lived with them.

meta.tagline: Jinnah's Karachi home, kept as he left it.
meta.address: Fatima Jinnah Road, Civil Lines, Karachi
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: Jinnah's study, drawing room and bedroom
His suits, sherwanis and Jinnah caps
Personal belongings of Fatima Jinnah
The garden and the colonial architecture

museums.title: Wazir Mansion
museums.excerpt: The birthplace of Quaid-e-Azam in old Karachi.
museums.content:
Muhammad Ali Jinnah was born in this stone house in the old Kharadar quarter of Karachi in 1876. It was declared a national monument and is now a museum and library.

The upper floors keep furniture, law books and belongings of the Jinnah family, and the narrow streets around it show how the old port city looked in the nineteenth century.

meta.tagline: The birthplace of Quaid-e-Azam in old Karachi.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: The room where Jinnah was born
Furniture and belongings of the Jinnah family
Jinnah's law books and papers
The old Kharadar neighbourhood around the house

museums.title: Mohatta Palace Museum
museums.excerpt: A pink stone palace by the Arabian Sea.
museums.content:
The businessman Shivratan Mohatta built this summer palace in 1927 from pink Jodhpur stone and yellow Gizri stone, in the style of the palaces of Rajasthan. After independence it housed the Foreign Office, and later Fatima Jinnah lived here.

It opened as a museum of art and culture in 1999 and holds changing exhibitions on the arts, crafts and history of Pakistan, inside one of Karachi's most beautiful buildings.

meta.tagline: A pink stone palace by the Arabian Sea.
meta.hours: Usually closed on Mondays. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: The palace architecture, with domes, balconies and carved stone
Changing exhibitions on Pakistani art and history
The rooftop pavilions
Gardens at the front of the palace

museums.title: Swat Museum
museums.excerpt: Buddhist treasures from the valley of Udyana.
museums.content:
Swat was the ancient land of Udyana, full of Buddhist monasteries and stupas, and pilgrims came here from as far as China. The Swat Museum holds Gandhara sculpture from sites across the valley, many excavated by Italian archaeologists.

The museum was badly damaged by a bomb in 2008, then rebuilt and reopened with help from Italy and Japan. Today it shows Buddhist sculpture, local jewellery, textiles and woodwork.

meta.tagline: Buddhist treasures from the valley of Udyana.
meta.address: Saidu Sharif Road, Swat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee; separate rate for foreign visitors.
highlights: Gandhara sculpture from Butkara and other Swat sites
Relief panels from Buddhist stupas
Swati jewellery, embroidery and carved wood
Stupas and rock carvings in the surrounding valley

museums.title: Pakistan Army Museum
museums.excerpt: Arms, uniforms and battles from the Mughals to today.
museums.content:
Founded in 1961, the Army Museum in Rawalpindi tells the history of soldiering in the subcontinent, from Mughal swords and armour to the wars fought by Pakistan since 1947.

Indoor galleries show weapons, medals, uniforms and paintings, and the outdoor park displays tanks, guns and aircraft. A gallery honours the soldiers awarded the Nishan-e-Haider.

meta.tagline: Arms, uniforms and battles from the Mughals to today.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: Mughal and Sikh swords, shields and armour
The Nishan-e-Haider gallery
Tanks and artillery in the outdoor park
Uniforms and medals across two centuries

museums.title: PAF Museum
museums.excerpt: Fighter jets, history and a park full of aircraft.
museums.content:
The Pakistan Air Force Museum tells the story of the air force from 1947 onward. Its large park displays fighter jets, transport aircraft, helicopters and radars, many of which you can walk right up to.

Indoor halls show uniforms, models and paintings of famous air battles, along with aircraft from the early years of Pakistan.

meta.tagline: Fighter jets, history and a park full of aircraft.
meta.hours: Open daily, including evenings. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: Fighter jets from the 1950s to recent decades
The hangar of historic aircraft
Galleries of PAF heroes and air battles
A family-friendly park popular in the evenings

museums.title: Pakistan Maritime Museum
museums.excerpt: Climb aboard a submarine that made history in 1971.
museums.content:
Run by the Pakistan Navy, the Maritime Museum covers the sea history of the region, from the ancient ports of the Indus to the modern navy.

The star exhibit is the submarine PNS Hangor, which sank the Indian frigate INS Khukri in the 1971 war. Visitors can go inside it, and the park also shows a minesweeper, aircraft and ship models.

meta.tagline: Climb aboard a submarine that made history in 1971.
meta.address: Habib Ibrahim Rehmatullah Road, Karsaz, Karachi
meta.hours: Open daily, including evenings. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee; extra ticket for the submarine.
highlights: The submarine PNS Hangor, open to visitors
A minesweeper and naval aircraft in the park
Galleries of ship models and naval history
A lake and park popular with families

museums.title: Pakistan Museum of Natural History
museums.excerpt: Fossils, minerals and wildlife of Pakistan.
museums.content:
Founded in 1976, the museum collects and studies the plants, animals, rocks and fossils of Pakistan. It is popular with school groups and families.

Highlights include fossils from the Siwalik hills, a whale skeleton, gemstones from the northern mountains and dioramas of Pakistan's wildlife, from the markhor to the Indus river dolphin.

meta.tagline: Fossils, minerals and wildlife of Pakistan.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Small entry fee.
highlights: Fossils of ancient mammals from the Siwalik hills
A large whale skeleton
Gemstones and minerals from the north
Wildlife dioramas, including the markhor

museums.title: British Museum
museums.excerpt: Two million years of human history in Bloomsbury.
museums.content:
Founded in 1753 from the collection of the physician Sir Hans Sloane and opened in 1759, the British Museum was the first national public museum in the world. Its collection of around eight million objects covers every continent.

Many objects came to London during the age of the British Empire, and the museum is at the centre of debates about returning them, from the Parthenon sculptures to the Benin Bronzes.

meta.tagline: Two million years of human history in Bloomsbury.
meta.hours: Open daily, usually 10:00 to 17:00. Check before you go.
meta.tickets: Free; some special exhibitions need a ticket.
highlights: The Rosetta Stone, the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs
The Parthenon sculptures from Athens
Egyptian mummies and the Assyrian lion-hunt reliefs
The Sutton Hoo treasure and the Lewis Chessmen

museums.title: Louvre Museum
museums.excerpt: A royal palace turned into the world's most visited museum.
museums.content:
The Louvre was a fortress and then a palace of the kings of France before it opened as a public museum in 1793, during the French Revolution. Today it is the most visited museum in the world.

Its galleries run from ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt to European painting of the nineteenth century, and its Department of Islamic Art is one of the finest in Europe. I. M. Pei's glass pyramid has been the entrance since 1989.

meta.tagline: A royal palace turned into the world's most visited museum.
meta.hours: Closed on Tuesdays. Book a timed ticket in advance.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; booking ahead is strongly recommended.
highlights: Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa
The Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace
The Code of Hammurabi
The Department of Islamic Art

museums.title: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
museums.excerpt: 5,000 years of art on Fifth Avenue.
museums.content:
Founded in 1870, the Met is the largest art museum in the United States. Its collection of more than a million and a half works spans every period and culture, from ancient Egypt to modern design.

It is famous for its Egyptian Temple of Dendur, its arms and armour halls, and its galleries of the art of the Arab lands, Turkey, Iran, Central Asia and later South Asia.

meta.tagline: 5,000 years of art on Fifth Avenue.
meta.hours: Closed on Wednesdays. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; pay what you wish for New York State residents.
highlights: The Temple of Dendur, an Egyptian temple rebuilt inside the museum
Arms and Armor galleries with mounted knights
Galleries of Islamic art, including Mughal works
European paintings by Rembrandt, Vermeer and Van Gogh

museums.title: Grand Egyptian Museum
museums.excerpt: Tutankhamun's full treasure, beside the Pyramids of Giza.
museums.content:
Built on the edge of the Giza plateau, the Grand Egyptian Museum is the largest museum in the world devoted to a single civilization. It opened fully in November 2025 after two decades of construction.

For the first time, the complete treasure of Tutankhamun is shown together. Visitors enter past a colossal statue of Ramesses II and climb a grand staircase lined with kings and gods, with the pyramids framed in the windows at the top.

meta.tagline: Tutankhamun's full treasure, beside the Pyramids of Giza.
meta.address: Alexandria Desert Road, near the Giza Pyramids
meta.hours: Open daily. Book tickets in advance.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; separate rates for Egyptians and foreign visitors.
highlights: The complete Tutankhamun collection, including his gold mask
The 3,200-year-old colossal statue of Ramesses II
The Grand Staircase of royal statues
The restored solar boat of King Khufu

museums.title: Egyptian Museum, Cairo
museums.excerpt: The old pink palace of the pharaohs on Tahrir Square.
museums.content:
Opened in 1902 in its famous pink building on Tahrir Square, the Egyptian Museum was for more than a century the home of the world's greatest collection of ancient Egyptian art.

The royal mummies moved to the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in 2021 and Tutankhamun's treasure went to the Grand Egyptian Museum, but the old museum still holds thousands of statues, coffins and papyri from every period of pharaonic history.

meta.tagline: The old pink palace of the pharaohs on Tahrir Square.
meta.hours: Open daily. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; separate rates for Egyptians and foreign visitors.
highlights: The Narmer Palette, from the very start of Egyptian history
Statues of Khafre and of Rahotep and Nofret
Treasures of the royal tombs of Tanis
The historic building and its central atrium

museums.title: Topkapi Palace Museum
museums.excerpt: Four centuries of Ottoman sultans above the Bosphorus.
museums.content:
Mehmed II, the conqueror of Constantinople, began this palace after 1453, and for about four hundred years it was the home and seat of government of the Ottoman sultans. It became a museum in 1924, soon after the end of the empire.

Visitors walk through courtyards, kiosks and the Harem, and see the imperial treasury, the kitchens with their Chinese porcelain, and the Chamber of Sacred Relics.

meta.tagline: Four centuries of Ottoman sultans above the Bosphorus.
meta.hours: Usually closed on Tuesdays. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; the Harem needs a separate ticket.
highlights: The Topkapi Dagger and the Spoonmaker's Diamond
The Chamber of Sacred Relics
The Harem and the Imperial Hall
Views over the Bosphorus and the Golden Horn

museums.title: Istanbul Archaeology Museums
museums.excerpt: The Ottoman Empire's first museum, in the palace gardens.
museums.content:
Opened in 1891 by the painter and archaeologist Osman Hamdi Bey, these three museums stand in the outer gardens of Topkapi Palace. They hold over a million objects from the lands of the Ottoman Empire.

The collection runs from the Hittites and ancient Greece to Rome and Byzantium, and includes the oldest known peace treaty and some of the finest carved sarcophagi of the ancient world.

meta.tagline: The Ottoman Empire's first museum, in the palace gardens.
meta.hours: Open daily. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket.
highlights: The Alexander Sarcophagus
The Treaty of Kadesh tablet, the oldest known peace treaty
The Tiled Kiosk, built for Mehmed II in 1472
Roman and Byzantine sculpture of Constantinople

museums.title: Vatican Museums
museums.excerpt: Michelangelo's ceiling and the art of the popes.
museums.content:
The museums trace their start to 1506, when Pope Julius II put the newly found Laocoon statue on display. Over five centuries the popes built up one of the greatest art collections on earth.

A visit ends in the Sistine Chapel, where Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512 and the Last Judgment decades later.

meta.tagline: Michelangelo's ceiling and the art of the popes.
meta.hours: Usually closed on Sundays, except the last Sunday of the month. Book ahead.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; booking ahead is strongly recommended.
highlights: The Sistine Chapel ceiling and the Last Judgment
The Raphael Rooms
The Laocoon and the Apollo Belvedere
The Gallery of Maps

museums.title: Capitoline Museums
museums.excerpt: The world's oldest public museum, on Rome's sacred hill.
museums.content:
In 1471 Pope Sixtus IV gave a group of ancient bronzes to the people of Rome, and the Capitoline Museums are often called the oldest public museum in the world. They stand on the Capitoline Hill, around a square designed by Michelangelo.

The collection is the story of Rome itself: its founding legend, its emperors and the everyday life of the ancient city, with a view over the Roman Forum from the galleries.

meta.tagline: The world's oldest public museum, on Rome's sacred hill.
meta.hours: Open daily. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket.
highlights: The Capitoline Wolf, symbol of Rome
The bronze horseman statue of Marcus Aurelius
The giant head and hand of Constantine
The view over the Roman Forum

museums.title: National Museum, New Delhi
museums.excerpt: From the Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro to Mughal miniatures.
museums.content:
The National Museum grew out of a 1947-48 exhibition of Indian art in London and opened in 1949. It holds over 200,000 objects covering five thousand years of South Asian history.

Its Harappan gallery holds the bronze Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro, and its painting galleries hold some of the finest Mughal miniatures and manuscripts anywhere.

meta.tagline: From the Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro to Mughal miniatures.
meta.hours: Usually closed on Mondays. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; separate rate for foreign visitors.
highlights: The bronze Dancing Girl from Mohenjo-daro
Mughal miniature paintings and manuscripts
Buddhist relics and sculpture
Arms and armour of the Mughal and Rajput courts

museums.title: Salar Jung Museum
museums.excerpt: One family's collection from the court of Hyderabad.
museums.content:
Nawab Mir Yousuf Ali Khan, Salar Jung III, served as prime minister of the Nizam of Hyderabad and spent his life collecting art from across the world. His collection opened to the public in 1951.

It ranges from Persian carpets and jade daggers to European statues and clocks, and is one of the largest one-man collections ever assembled.

meta.tagline: One family's collection from the court of Hyderabad.
meta.address: Salar Jung Road, on the Musi river, Hyderabad, India
meta.hours: Usually closed on Fridays. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; separate rate for foreign visitors.
highlights: The Veiled Rebecca, a marble statue by Benzoni
The English musical clock that strikes every hour
Jade and jewelled daggers of the Mughal emperors
Manuscripts and Qurans in fine calligraphy

museums.title: Museum of Islamic Art, Doha
museums.excerpt: 1,400 years of Islamic art in I. M. Pei's desert fortress.
museums.content:
Designed by I. M. Pei, who came out of retirement for it, the museum opened in 2008 on its own island off the Doha Corniche. Its geometric stone form was inspired by the ablution fountain of the Ibn Tulun Mosque in Cairo.

The collection spans three continents and fourteen centuries, from early Qurans to Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal court art, and was redisplayed in 2022.

meta.tagline: 1,400 years of Islamic art in I. M. Pei's desert fortress.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Check the museum website for current entry rules.
highlights: Pages from the Blue Quran
Mughal jewels, jades and daggers
Ottoman, Safavid and Mamluk metalwork and ceramics
The building itself and its view of the Doha skyline

museums.title: State Hermitage Museum
museums.excerpt: Catherine the Great's collection in the Winter Palace.
museums.content:
Catherine the Great began the collection in 1764 by buying a group of paintings from Berlin. It grew into one of the largest museums in the world, spread across the Winter Palace of the Russian tsars and the buildings beside it.

Its rooms hold paintings by Rembrandt and Leonardo, Scythian gold, and treasures from Central Asia, Iran and the Islamic world.

meta.tagline: Catherine the Great's collection in the Winter Palace.
meta.hours: Usually closed on Mondays. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket.
highlights: The state rooms of the Winter Palace
The Peacock Clock
Scythian gold from the steppe
Paintings by Rembrandt, Leonardo and Matisse

museums.title: Rijksmuseum
museums.excerpt: Rembrandt, Vermeer and the Dutch Golden Age.
museums.content:
Founded in 1800 and housed since 1885 in a palace-like building by Pierre Cuypers, the Rijksmuseum is the national museum of the Netherlands.

It tells the story of Dutch art and history, with the masterpieces of the seventeenth-century Golden Age at its heart.

meta.tagline: Rembrandt, Vermeer and the Dutch Golden Age.
meta.hours: Open daily, usually 9:00 to 17:00. Check before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; booking a time slot is recommended.
highlights: Rembrandt's The Night Watch
Vermeer's The Milkmaid
Dutch dollhouses and ship models
The library, one of the most beautiful in the world

museums.title: Acropolis Museum
museums.excerpt: The Parthenon's treasures, in sight of the Parthenon.
museums.content:
Opened in 2009 at the foot of the Acropolis, the museum holds the sculptures and objects found on the sacred rock. Glass floors let visitors look down onto the ruins of an ancient Athenian neighbourhood beneath it.

The top floor recreates the frieze of the Parthenon at its real size and angle, with the temple itself visible through the windows. Spaces are left for the pieces still in London.

meta.tagline: The Parthenon's treasures, in sight of the Parthenon.
meta.hours: Open daily. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket.
highlights: The Caryatids of the Erechtheion
The Parthenon Gallery with its frieze
Archaic statues of young women, the korai
The excavation visible beneath the glass floor

museums.title: Neues Museum
museums.excerpt: Nefertiti, rebuilt from the ruins of war.
museums.content:
Opened in 1855 on Berlin's Museum Island, the Neues Museum was bombed in the Second World War and stood in ruins for decades. The architect David Chipperfield rebuilt it, keeping the scars of war, and it reopened in 2009.

It is home to Berlin's Egyptian collection and its museum of prehistory, including one of the most famous portraits ever made.

meta.tagline: Nefertiti, rebuilt from the ruins of war.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; a time slot is required.
highlights: The painted bust of Queen Nefertiti
The Berlin Gold Hat from the Bronze Age
Papyri and Egyptian sculpture
The restored building with its wartime scars

museums.title: National Palace Museum
museums.excerpt: Treasures of the Chinese emperors, carried across the sea.
museums.content:
The collection began in the Forbidden City in Beijing. During the wars of the twentieth century it was packed into crates and moved again and again, and part of it reached Taiwan in 1948-49. The museum in Taipei opened in 1965.

It holds hundreds of thousands of objects from eight thousand years of Chinese history: bronzes, jades, porcelain, painting and calligraphy.

meta.tagline: Treasures of the Chinese emperors, carried across the sea.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket.
highlights: The Jadeite Cabbage
The Meat-shaped Stone
Song dynasty landscape paintings
Ancient bronze ritual vessels

museums.title: Louvre Abu Dhabi
museums.excerpt: A rain of light under a floating dome.
museums.content:
Opened in 2017 under an agreement with France, Louvre Abu Dhabi was designed by Jean Nouvel. Its great dome of layered stars lets sunlight fall through in a "rain of light" onto a little city of galleries by the sea.

Instead of separating cultures, its galleries show objects from different civilizations side by side, telling one story of humanity from the first villages to today.

meta.tagline: A rain of light under a floating dome.
meta.hours: Usually closed on Mondays. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket.
highlights: The dome and its rain of light
Galleries that set world cultures side by side
Loans from the Louvre and other French museums
Walkways by the water on Saadiyat Island

museums.title: National Museum of Iran
museums.excerpt: Persepolis, Susa and seven thousand years of Persia.
museums.content:
The museum's first building opened in 1937, with a great brick entrance arch inspired by the Sasanian palace of Ctesiphon. A second building for the Islamic period was added later.

Its galleries hold finds from Persepolis, Susa and other great sites of ancient Iran, from the Achaemenid kings to the Safavid shahs.

meta.tagline: Persepolis, Susa and seven thousand years of Persia.
meta.hours: Open most days. Check timings before you go.
meta.tickets: Paid ticket; separate rate for foreign visitors.
highlights: Reliefs and a bull capital from Persepolis
The Salt Men, preserved in an ancient salt mine
Achaemenid gold and silver
Islamic-era ceramics, tiles and manuscripts
