cities.title: Mohenjo-daro
cities.excerpt: Around 2500 BCE, on the banks of the Indus, people built one of the world's first planned cities: straight streets, baked-brick houses and covered drains.
cities.content:
Mohenjo-daro, "the mound of the dead" in Sindhi, was one of the largest cities of the Bronze Age. At its height it may have been home to around 40,000 people, living in a grid of streets laid out with remarkable care.

Almost every house had its own bathing area, and wastewater flowed into covered brick drains running along the streets. No palace or royal tomb has ever been found here, which still puzzles archaeologists: who ruled this city, and how?

The site was identified in 1922 by the archaeologist R. D. Banerji. Its writing, the Indus script, has never been deciphered, so the city's own name remains unknown.

meta.tagline: The great planned city of the Indus, with drains older than Rome.
highlights: The Great Bath, a waterproofed brick pool on the citadel mound
The citadel, later crowned by a Buddhist stupa of the Kushan era
The lower town's grid streets and covered drains
The "Priest-King" sculpture, now in the National Museum of Pakistan, Karachi
timeline: The city is laid out on the Indus floodplain
Decline begins as the Indus cities lose their trade and rivers shift
R. D. Banerji identifies the site
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Harappa
cities.excerpt: Harappa, beside an old course of the Ravi, was the first Indus city to be excavated, which is why the whole civilization is often called "Harappan".
cities.content:
People settled at Harappa more than five thousand years ago, and by 2600 BCE it had grown into a walled city with neighbourhoods built on separate mounds. Craftsmen here made beads of carnelian, shell bangles and the famous square stamp seals.

In the 1850s, long before anyone knew how old it was, engineers carried away its bricks to use as ballast for the Lahore to Multan railway. Much was lost, but enough survived for systematic excavation to begin in 1921 under Daya Ram Sahni.

Today a small museum on site displays pottery, seals, jewellery and toys found in the ruins.

meta.tagline: The city that gave a whole civilization its name.
highlights: Mound AB and Mound E, the city's raised neighbourhoods
The "Granary" or Great Hall on Mound F
Cemetery R37, one of the few Indus burial grounds
The Harappa Museum
timeline: First village on the site (Ravi phase)
Harappa becomes a major walled city
Bricks taken for the Lahore–Multan railway
Excavation begins under Daya Ram Sahni

cities.title: Taxila
cities.excerpt: Taxila sat where the roads from Central Asia met the plains of India. Persians, Mauryans, Greeks and Kushans each left a city here.
cities.content:
Taxila is not one city but three, built one after another in the same valley: the Bhir Mound, the Indo-Greek grid city of Sirkap, and the Kushan city of Sirsukh. Around them stand dozens of Buddhist stupas and monasteries.

Alexander the Great was welcomed here in 326 BCE. Later the city became a centre of learning in the Mauryan empire, and tradition links it with the scholar Chanakya. Under the Kushans, Gandhara artists carved Buddha figures that blended Greek and Indian styles.

Raids by the Hephthalites, or White Huns, in the 5th century CE brought Taxila's great age to an end.

meta.tagline: Crossroads of Persia, Greece and India, and a city of Buddhist learning.
highlights: Sirkap, with its main street and Double-Headed Eagle stupa
The Dharmarajika stupa
Jaulian monastery, high on a hill
Taxila Museum and its Gandhara sculptures
timeline: Bhir Mound city grows under Achaemenid influence
Alexander the Great is received at Taxila
Kushans build Sirsukh; Gandhara art flourishes
Hephthalite raids end the city's golden age

cities.title: Lahore
cities.excerpt: Ghaznavid sultans, Mughal emperors and Sikh maharajas all ruled from Lahore, and each left monuments that still stand in the Walled City.
cities.content:
Legend says Lahore was founded by Lava, son of Rama, but the city enters written history around the 11th century, when it became a seat of the Ghaznavid sultans. The Sufi saint Ali Hujwiri, Data Ganj Bakhsh, lived and is buried here.

Under the Mughals Lahore reached its golden age. Akbar held court here, Shah Jahan laid out the Shalimar Gardens, and Aurangzeb built the Badshahi Mosque, for centuries the largest mosque in the world. Later, Maharaja Ranjit Singh made it the capital of the Sikh empire.

The thirteen gates of the old Walled City still lead into lanes of bazaars, havelis and food streets.

meta.tagline: Mughal capital, city of gardens, and the beating heart of Punjab.
highlights: Lahore Fort (Shahi Qila) and its Sheesh Mahal
Badshahi Mosque, completed in 1673
Wazir Khan Mosque and its tile work
Shalimar Gardens, laid out in 1641–42
timeline: Akbar rules the Mughal empire from Lahore
Badshahi Mosque is completed under Aurangzeb
Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens listed by UNESCO

cities.title: Multan
cities.excerpt: Multan is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of South Asia, famous for its Sufi shrines, blue tiles and fierce summers.
cities.content:
Multan was already an important city when Alexander's army fought the Malli in this region in 326 BCE. It was renowned for its Sun Temple, which drew pilgrims from across the subcontinent.

In 712–713 CE Muhammad bin Qasim took the city, and it became one of the first centres of Islam in South Asia. Over the following centuries it was a frontier fortress for the Delhi Sultanate and a home for great Sufi teachers.

The tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, built in the early 14th century, rises over the old fort mound and is one of the finest brick monuments in Pakistan.

meta.tagline: The City of Saints, inhabited for well over two thousand years.
highlights: Tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam
Shrine of Bahauddin Zakariya
Qasim Bagh, the old fort mound
Ghanta Ghar and the old bazaars
timeline: Alexander campaigns against the Malli in the region
Bahauddin Zakariya makes Multan a great Sufi centre
Tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam is built

cities.title: Thatta & Makli
cities.excerpt: For three centuries Thatta was the capital of lower Sindh. On the ridge beside it, rulers, saints and scholars lie in the vast stone necropolis of Makli.
cities.content:
Thatta rose under the Samma dynasty in the 14th century and became a rich port and centre of learning on the Indus delta, later ruled by the Arghuns, Tarkhans and Mughals.

The Makli necropolis covers about ten square kilometres and holds hundreds of thousands of graves. Its carved sandstone tombs, like that of Jam Nizamuddin II, mix Hindu, Gujarati and Persian styles in a way found nowhere else.

In the town, the Shah Jahan Mosque, finished in 1647, has 93 domes and acoustics so good that a voice carries across the whole prayer hall.

meta.tagline: Old capital of Sindh, beside one of the largest necropolises on Earth.
highlights: Tomb of Jam Nizamuddin II at Makli
Tarkhan and Mughal tombs with Persian-style domes
Shah Jahan Mosque, with its blue and white tiles
Views over the Indus delta from the Makli ridge
timeline: Samma rulers make Thatta their capital
Tomb of Jam Nizamuddin II is built at Makli
Makli listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Babylon
cities.excerpt: On the Euphrates south of modern Baghdad, Babylon was for centuries the greatest city in the world and a byword for splendour.
cities.content:
Babylon first rose to power under King Hammurabi (c. 1792–1750 BCE), whose code of laws, carved on a black stone stele, is one of the oldest legal texts we have.

Its second golden age came under Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BCE), who rebuilt the city with huge double walls, the ziggurat Etemenanki, and the Ishtar Gate, faced with blue glazed bricks showing dragons and bulls. The Hanging Gardens may have stood here too, though no trace has been found.

Cyrus the Great of Persia took the city in 539 BCE, and Alexander the Great died in Nebuchadnezzar's palace in 323 BCE.

meta.tagline: City of Hammurabi's laws, Nebuchadnezzar's walls and the blue Ishtar Gate.
highlights: Ruins of Nebuchadnezzar's Southern Palace
Processional Way and the reconstructed Ishtar Gate
The Lion of Babylon basalt statue
The original Ishtar Gate, now in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin
timeline: Ishtar Gate is built by Nebuchadnezzar II
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Ur
cities.excerpt: Ur was one of the great Sumerian city-states. Its stepped ziggurat, built around 2100 BCE, is the best preserved in Mesopotamia.
cities.content:
In the third millennium BCE Ur stood near the mouth of the Euphrates and grew rich on trade that reached as far as the Indus Valley: Harappan beads and seals have been found here.

King Ur-Nammu built the Great Ziggurat around 2100 BCE as a temple platform for Nanna, the moon god. Between 1922 and 1934 Leonard Woolley excavated the Royal Tombs, finding gold helmets, lyres and the Standard of Ur.

Tradition identifies the city with "Ur of the Chaldees", the birthplace of the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham).

meta.tagline: Sumerian city of the moon god, with its great ziggurat still standing.
highlights: The Great Ziggurat of Ur
The Royal Tombs excavated by Woolley
The Standard of Ur, now in the British Museum
Remains of houses from the time of Abraham's tradition
timeline: Leonard Woolley excavates the Royal Tombs
Listed by UNESCO with the marshes of southern Iraq

cities.title: Persepolis
cities.excerpt: Darius the Great began Persepolis around 518 BCE as a stage for the Persian empire, where envoys from every land brought tribute to the king.
cities.content:
Persepolis, Parsa to the Persians, stands on a vast stone terrace at the foot of the Mountain of Mercy. Darius I began it, and Xerxes and Artaxerxes added halls whose cedar roofs were held up by forests of stone columns.

Carved staircases show delegations from across the empire, Indians, Ethiopians, Lydians and many more, carrying gifts. They give us a rare picture of the ancient world's many peoples in one place.

In 330 BCE Alexander the Great's army looted the city and burned its palaces. The columns and reliefs that survived are among the finest works of ancient Persia.

meta.tagline: Ceremonial capital of the Persian kings, burned by Alexander.
highlights: The Gate of All Nations built by Xerxes
The Apadana and its tribute-bearer reliefs
The Hall of a Hundred Columns
Royal tombs at nearby Naqsh-e Rustam
timeline: Xerxes adds the Gate of All Nations
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Petra
cities.excerpt: The Nabataeans grew rich on the incense trade and carved their capital, temples and tombs directly into the red sandstone of southern Jordan.
cities.content:
Petra is reached through the Siq, a narrow gorge more than a kilometre long. At its end the façade of Al-Khazneh, "the Treasury", suddenly appears, cut into the rock face nearly forty metres high.

The Nabataeans were masters of water. With channels, dams and cisterns they turned a desert valley into a city of perhaps 20,000 people that controlled caravan routes between Arabia, Egypt and Syria.

Rome annexed Petra in 106 CE. Trade routes shifted, an earthquake in 363 CE caused great damage, and the city faded until the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt described it to Europe in 1812.

meta.tagline: The rose-red city carved straight into the cliffs.
highlights: The Siq gorge and Al-Khazneh (the Treasury)
Ad Deir (the Monastery), up 800 rock-cut steps
The Royal Tombs
The Roman-style theatre carved from the rock
timeline: First written mention of the Nabataeans at Petra
Petra is annexed by the Roman Empire
A major earthquake damages the city
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Damascus
cities.excerpt: People have lived in Damascus for thousands of years. From 661 to 750 CE it was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, which stretched from Spain to Sindh.
cities.content:
Damascus grew in the Ghouta oasis, watered by the Barada river at the edge of the desert. Aramaeans, Persians, Greeks and Romans all ruled here, and the Roman grid can still be traced in the old city's Straight Street.

In 661 CE Muawiya made Damascus the capital of the Umayyad caliphate. Caliph al-Walid I built the Great Mosque between 705 and 715 CE on the site of a Roman temple and a church, decorating it with golden mosaics of gardens and rivers.

Salahuddin Ayyubi, who retook Jerusalem in 1187, is buried beside the Umayyad Mosque.

meta.tagline: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities, and capital of the Umayyads.
highlights: The Umayyad Mosque and its mosaics
Tomb of Salahuddin Ayyubi
Straight Street and the Roman arch
The Citadel and the Al-Hamidiyah Souq
timeline: Becomes capital of the Umayyad caliphate
Ancient City of Damascus listed by UNESCO

cities.title: Baghdad
cities.excerpt: Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762 CE as a perfect circle on the Tigris. Within a century it was one of the largest and most learned cities on Earth.
cities.content:
Al-Mansur named his capital Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Its three rings of walls had four gates facing the corners of the empire, with the caliph's palace and great mosque at the centre.

Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Here al-Khwarizmi wrote the book that gave us the word "algebra".

In 1258 the Mongols under Hulagu Khan sacked the city. Little of the Round City survives, but Baghdad lives on as Iraq's capital.

meta.tagline: The Round City of the Abbasids and home of the House of Wisdom.
highlights: Al-Mustansiriya Madrasa, built 1227–1234
The Abbasid Palace on the Tigris
Al-Mutanabbi Street, the old booksellers' market
The Kadhimiya shrine

cities.title: Athens
cities.excerpt: In the 5th century BCE this small city-state produced democracy, theatre and philosophy, and crowned its rock with the Parthenon.
cities.content:
The Acropolis rock was settled long before written history. In 508 BCE the reforms of Cleisthenes gave Athens a government by its citizens, the first democracy.

After the victory over Persia, Pericles rebuilt the Acropolis. The Parthenon, dedicated to the goddess Athena, was built between 447 and 432 BCE. In the same century Socrates questioned the young men of the Agora, and Plato and Aristotle followed.

Athens lived on under Romans, Byzantines and Ottomans, and became the capital of modern Greece in 1834.

meta.tagline: Birthplace of democracy, philosophy and the Parthenon.
highlights: The Parthenon and the Acropolis
The Erechtheion and its Caryatid columns
The Ancient Agora, where Socrates taught
The Theatre of Dionysus
timeline: The Acropolis is listed by UNESCO

cities.title: Pompeii
cities.excerpt: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii under metres of ash, preserving its streets, shops, paintings and even its graffiti.
cities.content:
Pompeii was a busy Roman town of perhaps 11,000 people near the Bay of Naples, with bakeries, bathhouses, taverns and an amphitheatre older than the Colosseum.

In 79 CE Vesuvius erupted. Within two days the town lay under pumice and ash. Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and wrote the only eyewitness account.

Excavation began in 1748. In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the hollows left by the victims' bodies, creating the haunting casts that visitors see today.

meta.tagline: A Roman town frozen in a single day by Vesuvius.
highlights: The Forum with Vesuvius behind it
The Villa of the Mysteries and its frescoes
The Amphitheatre, built around 70 BCE
The House of the Faun
timeline: Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Carthage
cities.excerpt: Founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, Carthage built a sea empire across the western Mediterranean and fought Rome in three great wars.
cities.content:
Legend says Queen Elissa, also called Dido, founded Carthage in 814 BCE. The city grew into a naval power, with a circular military harbour that could shelter more than a hundred warships.

In the Second Punic War Hannibal marched an army, with elephants, over the Alps into Italy and defeated Rome at Cannae in 216 BCE. Rome won in the end, and in 146 BCE destroyed Carthage completely.

Julius Caesar and Augustus refounded it as a Roman city, which became one of the largest in the empire. It was taken by the Vandals in 439 and by the Umayyads in 698.

meta.tagline: Hannibal's city, Rome's great rival across the sea.
highlights: Byrsa Hill, the old citadel
The Punic Ports, military and merchant harbours
The Antonine Baths by the sea
The Tophet, the ancient sacred precinct
timeline: The city is taken by the Umayyads

cities.title: Alexandria
cities.excerpt: Founded by Alexander the Great on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, Alexandria became the intellectual capital of the ancient world.
cities.content:
Alexander chose the site in 331 BCE. After his death his general Ptolemy made it the capital of Egypt, and the Ptolemies built the Mouseion and the Great Library, which tried to collect every book in the world.

The Pharos lighthouse, finished around 280 BCE, stood over a hundred metres tall and was counted among the Seven Wonders. Earthquakes destroyed it in the Middle Ages, and the Citadel of Qaitbay was built on its foundations in 1477.

Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemaic ruler, died here in 30 BCE. In 2002 the Bibliotheca Alexandrina opened as a modern tribute to the ancient library.

meta.tagline: Alexander's city of the Great Library and the Lighthouse.
highlights: The Citadel of Qaitbay, on the site of the Pharos
The Catacombs of Kom el Shoqafa
Pompey's Pillar and the Serapeum
The Bibliotheca Alexandrina
timeline: Alexander the Great founds the city
Death of Cleopatra; Egypt passes to Rome
Qaitbay builds his citadel on the Pharos site

cities.title: Thebes (Luxor)
cities.excerpt: For much of Egypt's New Kingdom, Thebes was the religious capital of the Pharaohs. Its temples and royal tombs make it the world's largest open-air museum.
cities.content:
On the east bank of the Nile, the "city of the living", stand the temples of Karnak and Luxor, linked by an avenue of sphinxes. Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 giant columns.

On the west bank, the "city of the dead", Pharaohs were buried in tombs cut deep into the Valley of the Kings, and queens such as Hatshepsut built great mortuary temples.

In 1922 Howard Carter found the almost untouched tomb of the young king Tutankhamun here, one of the most famous discoveries in archaeology.

meta.tagline: Capital of the Pharaohs, with the Valley of the Kings across the Nile.
highlights: Karnak Temple and its Hypostyle Hall
Luxor Temple and the Avenue of Sphinxes
The Valley of the Kings
The Temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari
timeline: Thebes rises as a royal capital

cities.title: Constantinople (Istanbul)
cities.excerpt: For over 1,500 years this city on the Bosphorus was the capital first of the Eastern Roman Empire and then of the Ottomans.
cities.content:
Greek colonists founded Byzantium on the Bosphorus around 657 BCE. In 330 CE Emperor Constantine made it the new capital of the Roman Empire, Constantinople, and protected it with walls that held for a thousand years.

Emperor Justinian completed the Hagia Sophia in 537 CE; its dome seemed to float on light and remained the largest in the world for centuries.

On 29 May 1453 the 21-year-old Sultan Mehmed II took the city after a long siege, and it became the Ottoman capital, crowned with mosques by the architect Mimar Sinan.

meta.tagline: The city on two continents, capital of two empires.
highlights: Hagia Sophia
The Theodosian Land Walls
The Basilica Cistern
Topkapı Palace and the Süleymaniye Mosque
timeline: Constantine makes it the Roman capital
Sultan Mehmed II conquers the city

cities.title: Samarkand
cities.excerpt: One of the oldest cities of Central Asia, Samarkand reached its peak as the capital of Amir Timur, who filled it with blue-tiled domes and madrasas.
cities.content:
Ancient Maracanda was a Sogdian trading city when Alexander the Great took it in 329 BCE. For centuries its merchants carried silk, paper and spices between China, India and Persia.

Genghis Khan's army destroyed it in 1220, but in 1370 Amir Timur made Samarkand his capital and brought craftsmen from every land he conquered to rebuild it.

His grandson Ulugh Beg, an astronomer-king, built a madrasa on the Registan and an observatory whose star tables were the most accurate of their age.

meta.tagline: Timur's turquoise capital at the heart of the Silk Road.
highlights: The Registan and its three madrasas
Gur-e-Amir, Timur's mausoleum
Bibi-Khanym Mosque
Shah-i-Zinda necropolis and Ulugh Beg's observatory
timeline: Amir Timur makes Samarkand his capital
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Bukhara
cities.excerpt: Bukhara was the capital of the Samanids and one of the great centres of Islamic learning, with over a hundred madrasas at its height.
cities.content:
In the 9th and 10th centuries the Samanid rulers made Bukhara a capital of Persian culture. The poet Rudaki wrote here, and the young Ibn Sina, born near Bukhara in 980, studied in the royal library.

Imam Muhammad al-Bukhari, compiler of the Sahih al-Bukhari, was born in the city in 810 CE.

The Kalyan Minaret, built in 1127, so impressed Genghis Khan that he spared it when he burned the city in 1220. Much of the old centre still stands, around the Lyab-i Hauz pool.

meta.tagline: The holy city of scholars, home town of Imam al-Bukhari.
highlights: Ismail Samani Mausoleum, early 10th century
Po-i-Kalyan complex and the Kalyan Minaret
The Ark fortress
Lyab-i Hauz and the trading domes
timeline: Imam al-Bukhari is born in the city

cities.title: Merv
cities.excerpt: Merv grew in an oasis of the Karakum desert. In the 12th century, as capital of the Great Seljuks, it may have been the biggest city on Earth.
cities.content:
Merv is a set of walled cities side by side, built over 2,000 years as the settlement moved across the oasis: Erk Kala, Gyaur Kala, Sultan Kala and others.

Under the Seljuk Sultan Sanjar in the 12th century Merv was a city of libraries, observatories and gardens. His mausoleum, finished around 1157, still stands with its great double dome.

In 1221 the Mongols under Tolui, son of Genghis Khan, destroyed the city and killed most of its people. Merv never recovered.

meta.tagline: Seljuk capital that was briefly the largest city in the world.
highlights: The Mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar
Erk Kala, the oldest fortress
The walls of Gyaur Kala and Sultan Kala
The Great and Little Kyz Kala, corrugated mud-brick castles
timeline: Mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar is completed
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Chang'an (Xi'an)
cities.excerpt: Chang'an, "Perpetual Peace", was the capital of China's Han and Tang dynasties and the starting point of the Silk Road caravans heading west.
cities.content:
The Han emperors made Chang'an their capital in 202 BCE. Nearby lies the tomb of the First Emperor, Qin Shi Huang, guarded by the Terracotta Army that farmers found while digging a well in 1974.

Under the Tang dynasty (618–907) Chang'an may have had a million people, with markets where Persian, Sogdian and Arab merchants traded. The monk Xuanzang returned here from India in 645 with Buddhist texts and built the Big Wild Goose Pagoda to keep them.

Today's Xi'an is still ringed by its Ming-era city walls, among the best preserved in China.

meta.tagline: Eastern gate of the Silk Road and capital of the Han and Tang.
highlights: The Terracotta Army
The Big Wild Goose Pagoda, first built in 652
The Ming city walls
The Great Mosque of Xi'an
timeline: Han dynasty makes Chang'an its capital
Big Wild Goose Pagoda is built for Xuanzang
Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor listed by UNESCO

cities.title: Machu Picchu
cities.excerpt: Built around 1450 for the Inca emperor Pachacuti, Machu Picchu sits on a mountain ridge 2,430 metres above sea level.
cities.content:
Inca builders shaped granite blocks so precisely that they fit together without mortar. Terraces carved into the slopes grew crops and held the mountain together in heavy rains.

The site was probably a royal estate. It was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest, and the conquistadors never found it.

Local farmers always knew it was there, but it became famous worldwide after the American explorer Hiram Bingham was guided to it in 1911.

meta.tagline: The Inca citadel in the clouds above the Urubamba.
highlights: The Temple of the Sun
The Intihuatana stone
The Room of the Three Windows
The climb up Huayna Picchu
timeline: Hiram Bingham brings it to world attention
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Teotihuacan
cities.excerpt: Around 450 CE Teotihuacan was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 100,000 people. We still do not know what its builders called themselves.
cities.content:
The city was laid out along the Avenue of the Dead, more than two kilometres long, lined with temples and platforms. The Pyramid of the Sun, one of the largest in the Americas, was built around 200 CE.

Its influence reached far into the Maya lands, and its apartment compounds housed people from across Mesoamerica.

Around 550 CE the city centre was burned, and Teotihuacan declined. Centuries later the Aztecs found its ruins and named it "the place where the gods were created".

meta.tagline: The city of the gods and its Pyramid of the Sun.
highlights: The Pyramid of the Sun
The Pyramid of the Moon
The Avenue of the Dead
The Temple of the Feathered Serpent
timeline: The Pyramid of the Sun is built
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Angkor
cities.excerpt: From the 9th to the 15th century Angkor was the heart of the Khmer empire, a vast city of temples, reservoirs and canals in the Cambodian forest.
cities.content:
The Khmer kingdom traditionally dates its founding to 802 CE, when Jayavarman II declared himself universal monarch. Over the next centuries kings built huge reservoirs, called barays, to water the rice fields that fed the city.

King Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat in the early 12th century. Its five lotus-bud towers represent Mount Meru, the centre of the universe in Hindu belief.

Later, Jayavarman VII built the walled city of Angkor Thom, whose Bayon temple is covered with more than two hundred giant smiling stone faces.

meta.tagline: Capital of the Khmer empire and the largest religious monument on Earth.
highlights: Angkor Wat at sunrise
The Bayon and its stone faces
Ta Prohm, wrapped in tree roots
The gates of Angkor Thom
timeline: Jayavarman II founds the Khmer empire
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

cities.title: Chichen Itza
cities.excerpt: Chichen Itza was one of the largest Maya cities of the Yucatán, famous for its stepped pyramid, El Castillo, and its sacred well.
cities.content:
The city flourished from around 600 to 1200 CE, drawing people from across the Maya world. Its name means "at the mouth of the well of the Itza", after the great natural sinkhole, the Sacred Cenote.

El Castillo, the Temple of Kukulcan, has 91 steps on each of its four sides; with the top platform they add up to 365, the days of the year. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the afternoon sun casts a shadow like a serpent sliding down the stairs.

The Great Ball Court here is the largest known in ancient Mesoamerica.

meta.tagline: The Maya city where a serpent of light descends the pyramid.
highlights: El Castillo (Temple of Kukulcan)
The Great Ball Court
The Sacred Cenote
El Caracol, the round observatory
timeline: The city is at its height
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

castles.title: Lahore Fort
castles.excerpt: The Shahi Qila of Lahore grew over a century of Mughal rule, from Akbar's brick fortress to Shah Jahan's marble palaces and the mirror-work of the Sheesh Mahal.
castles.content:
A fort stood on this rise beside the Ravi long before the Mughals, but the Lahore Fort we see today began in 1566, when Emperor Akbar rebuilt it in brick as a base for his northern campaigns. Each emperor after him added his own palace, hall or garden, so walking through the fort is like turning the pages of Mughal history.

Jahangir added quarters and began the famous Picture Wall, covered in tile and fresco scenes of elephants, polo matches and hunts. Shah Jahan built the white marble halls, the Naulakha Pavilion and the Sheesh Mahal, the Palace of Mirrors, whose ceilings glitter with thousands of tiny pieces of glass. Aurangzeb gave the fort its grand Alamgiri Gate, facing the Badshahi Mosque.

Later, Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled from here, and the British used it as a garrison. In 1981 UNESCO listed the fort, together with the Shalimar Gardens, as a World Heritage Site.

castles.title: Rohtas Fort
castles.excerpt: After defeating the Mughal emperor Humayun, Sher Shah Suri built Rohtas to guard the road to Kabul and keep the Gakhar tribes in check. Its walls run for about four kilometres.
castles.content:
In 1540 Sher Shah Suri drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India. To stop him from coming back through the north-west, and to control the local Gakhar chiefs who supported him, Sher Shah ordered a massive fort on the Grand Trunk Road near Jhelum. Work began in 1541 under his minister Raja Todar Mal.

Rohtas is all about defence. Its stone walls run for about four kilometres, with 68 bastions and 12 gates. The Sohail Gate and the Kabuli Gate are the grandest, and the step-wells inside could supply a large garrison during a siege.

Sher Shah died in 1545, before the fort was finished, and when Humayun returned in 1555 the fort was handed over without a fight. Because it was never stormed, it survives as one of the finest examples of early Muslim military architecture in South Asia, and UNESCO listed it in 1997.

castles.title: Derawar Fort
castles.excerpt: Derawar's forty bastions can be seen for miles across the Cholistan Desert. First raised by a Bhatti Rajput prince, it was taken and rebuilt by the Abbasi Nawabs of Bahawalpur in the 1730s.
castles.content:
Out in the Cholistan Desert, some 130 kilometres from Bahawalpur, Derawar Fort rises like a mountain of brick. Tradition says it was first built in the 9th century by Rai Jajja Bhatti, a Rajput prince, and named after his relative Rawal Deoraj of Jaisalmer, from "Dera Rawal".

In 1733 the fort was taken by Nawab Sadiq Muhammad Khan Abbasi, and the Abbasi Nawabs of Bahawalpur rebuilt it in its present form. Its walls stand about 30 metres high, with forty round bastions, ten on each side, and a perimeter of around one and a half kilometres.

Beside the fort stands a white marble mosque modelled on the Moti Masjid in Delhi's Red Fort, and nearby is the royal graveyard of the Abbasi family. Every winter the Cholistan Desert Jeep Rally roars past its walls.

castles.title: Ranikot Fort
castles.excerpt: Ranikot's walls run for around 30 kilometres over the bare Kirthar hills, making it one of the largest forts in the world. Its present walls were rebuilt by the Talpur Mirs in 1812.
castles.content:
Ranikot is so big that it is often called the Great Wall of Sindh. Its walls climb and dip across the rugged Kirthar hills for around 30 kilometres, enclosing whole valleys, streams and smaller forts inside.

Nobody knows exactly who first built it. Historians have suggested Sassanian, Arab and local origins, but the walls we see today were largely rebuilt in 1812 by the Talpur Mirs, the rulers of Sindh, as a refuge and a guard on the western routes.

Inside are two smaller forts, Miri Kot and Shergarh. Ranikot has been on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites since 1993, and it makes a popular day trip from Karachi and Hyderabad.

castles.title: Baltit Fort
castles.excerpt: Perched above Karimabad with Rakaposhi on the horizon, Baltit Fort was the seat of the Mirs of Hunza for centuries. Restored in the 1990s, it is now a museum.
castles.content:
Baltit Fort sits on a rocky shelf above Karimabad, looking across the Hunza valley to the snowy peak of Rakaposhi. Built of stone and timber more than 700 years ago and enlarged many times since, it was the palace and stronghold of the Mirs, the rulers of Hunza.

A popular story says that a Hunza prince married a princess from Baltistan, and she brought Balti craftsmen with her to rebuild the fort, which is how it got its name. Its wooden beams and stone layers were designed to flex during the earthquakes that shake these mountains.

In 1945 the Mir moved to a new palace below, and the old fort began to crumble. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture restored it between 1990 and 1996, and it reopened as a museum of Hunza's history and culture.

castles.title: Altit Fort
castles.excerpt: Altit Fort clings to a cliff hundreds of metres above the Hunza River. Around a thousand years old, it is thought to be the oldest building in Gilgit-Baltistan.
castles.content:
Before Baltit, there was Altit. This fort stands at the edge of a sheer cliff that drops hundreds of metres to the Hunza River, and it is believed to be about a thousand years old, making it the oldest surviving building in Gilgit-Baltistan.

Its watchtower, the Shikari Tower, gave the rulers of Hunza a view far up and down the valley. Inside are small dark rooms, low doors and carved wooden windows, built to keep out the winter cold.

The Aga Khan Trust for Culture restored the fort and the old village around it, and it opened to visitors in 2007. The project was later honoured with a UNESCO Asia-Pacific award for heritage conservation. Its royal garden, with apricot and apple trees, is a peaceful place to rest.

castles.title: Shigar Fort
castles.excerpt: Shigar Fort, known locally as Fong-Khar, the palace on the rock, was the seat of the Amacha Rajas of Shigar. Restored by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, it now welcomes guests as a heritage hotel and museum.
castles.content:
At the mouth of the Shigar valley, on the old route towards K2, stands a fort built against a huge boulder. Local people call it Fong-Khar, the palace on the rock. It was built in the 17th century by Raja Hassan Khan of the Amacha dynasty, who ruled Shigar for generations.

Like other Balti buildings, it mixes thick stone walls with carved wooden balconies, beams and pillars. Some of its woodwork was brought from older buildings and is beautifully decorated.

The Aga Khan Trust for Culture restored the fort, and it opened in 2004 as a heritage hotel with a small museum, so visitors can sleep inside a Balti palace.

castles.title: Attock Fort
castles.excerpt: Emperor Akbar built Attock Fort beside the Indus crossing to control the road between Kabul and Lahore. It is still used by the army today and is closed to the public.
castles.content:
Where the Kabul River pours into the Indus, armies, traders and travellers have crossed for thousands of years. In 1581 Emperor Akbar ordered a strong fort here, built under the supervision of Khwaja Shamsuddin Khawafi and finished in about two years.

The fort helped Akbar guard his empire against his half-brother Mirza Muhammad Hakim, ruler of Kabul, and controlled the Grand Trunk Road. In 1813 the Sikh army under Ranjit Singh won the Battle of Attock nearby and took control of the crossing.

Attock Fort is still in military use, so visitors cannot go inside. Its long walls are best seen from the old Attock Bridge or the riverbank.

castles.title: Kot Diji Fort
castles.excerpt: Built by Mir Sohrab Khan Talpur, the founder of Khairpur State, Kot Diji Fort runs along a narrow limestone ridge. At its foot lies one of the oldest settlements of the Indus Valley.
castles.content:
Kot Diji Fort, also called Ahmadabad Fort, was built between 1785 and 1795 by Mir Sohrab Khan Talpur, the founder of the princely state of Khairpur. It stretches along the top of a narrow limestone ridge, with strong bastions and a single steep road up to its gate.

Its brick walls guarded Khairpur against attacks from the east, where the desert opens towards Rajasthan. Inside are the remains of the Mir's quarters, water tanks and gun platforms.

Right below the fort lies the archaeological site of Kot Diji, a town first settled around 3300 BCE, before the great cities of the Indus Valley. So in one visit you can see five thousand years of Sindh's history.

castles.title: Bala Hisar, Peshawar
castles.excerpt: Bala Hisar, the "high fort", stands on a mound above the old city of Peshawar, near the road to the Khyber Pass. Rulers from Babur to the Durranis and the Sikhs held it. Today it is the headquarters of the Frontier Corps.
castles.content:
Bala Hisar means "high fort" in Persian, and it stands on a mound above the old city of Peshawar, close to the road that leads to the Khyber Pass. The Mughal emperor Babur wrote about the fort in his memoirs in the early 16th century.

When Timur Shah Durrani made Peshawar his winter capital in the 18th century, Bala Hisar became a royal residence. The Sikhs took Peshawar in the 1830s and rebuilt the fort in 1834, and the British later strengthened it again.

Today Bala Hisar is the headquarters of the Frontier Corps, so it is not open like an ordinary monument, although a small museum inside can sometimes be visited with permission. Its high walls are a landmark of the city.

castles.title: Red Fort, Delhi
castles.excerpt: When Shah Jahan moved his capital from Agra to Delhi, he built the Red Fort as the heart of his new city, Shahjahanabad. For two centuries it was the palace of the Mughal emperors.
castles.content:
In 1639 Emperor Shah Jahan began a new capital at Delhi, called Shahjahanabad, and at its heart a walled palace of red sandstone beside the Yamuna River. The Red Fort, or Lal Qila, was finished in 1648, and its design is credited to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who is also linked to the Taj Mahal.

Inside the walls were marble halls, gardens and channels of flowing water. In the Diwan-i-Khas, the hall of private audience, stood the famous Peacock Throne, carried off by Nadir Shah of Persia in 1739. Its walls still bear the Persian verse: "If there is a paradise on earth, it is this, it is this, it is this."

After the uprising of 1857, the British exiled the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, and turned the fort into a barracks. UNESCO listed it in 2007.

castles.title: Mehrangarh Fort
castles.excerpt: Mehrangarh rises straight out of a rocky hill high above Jodhpur. Founded by Rao Jodha in 1459, it is one of the largest and most dramatic forts in India.
castles.content:
In 1459 Rao Jodha, chief of the Rathore Rajputs, moved his capital to a new site and began a fort on a steep hill called Bhakurcheeria, the mountain of birds. Around it grew the city of Jodhpur, whose old houses are painted blue.

The walls of Mehrangarh seem to grow out of the rock itself. Visitors enter through a series of seven gates, including the Jai Pol, built by Maharaja Man Singh in 1806 to celebrate victories over Jaipur and Bikaner, and the Fateh Pol, which marks a victory over the Mughals.

Inside are richly decorated palaces such as the Moti Mahal and Phool Mahal, and one of the best museums in Rajasthan, with palanquins, weapons and paintings of the Rathore rulers.

castles.title: Amber Fort
castles.excerpt: Raja Man Singh I, one of Akbar's greatest generals, began Amber Fort in 1592. Its palaces mix Rajput and Mughal styles, and its Sheesh Mahal sparkles with mirror-work.
castles.content:
Amber, or Amer, was the capital of the Kachwaha Rajputs long before Jaipur existed. In 1592 Raja Man Singh I, a trusted general of the Mughal emperor Akbar, began the palace-fort we see today on a hill above Maota Lake.

Built of pale yellow sandstone and white marble, its courtyards and halls blend Rajput and Mughal design. The Ganesh Pol gateway is painted with delicate patterns, and the Sheesh Mahal is covered in thousands of tiny mirrors that glow when a single candle is lit.

In 1727 Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur and moved the court there. In 2013 Amber became part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Hill Forts of Rajasthan".

castles.title: Citadel of Aleppo
castles.excerpt: The Citadel of Aleppo crowns a great hill in the middle of the city. People have worshipped and fortified here for some five thousand years, and its present walls and gate date mostly from around 1200.
castles.content:
In the middle of Aleppo rises a huge, partly man-made hill, wrapped in a stone slope and a deep moat. Excavations have found a temple of the ancient storm god on its summit dating back thousands of years, so this hill has been a sacred and royal place since about 3000 BCE.

Most of what stands today was built by az-Zahir Ghazi, a son of Saladin who ruled Aleppo around 1200. He gave the citadel its sloping glacis, its bridge and its mighty gateway, which twists several times to slow down attackers. After the Mongols and later Timur damaged it, the Mamluk sultans repaired it.

The citadel is part of the Ancient City of Aleppo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. It was damaged during the Syrian war and by the 2023 earthquake, and restoration work continues.

castles.title: Krak des Chevaliers
castles.excerpt: Krak des Chevaliers was the mightiest castle of the Crusader knights, with two rings of walls on a hilltop in western Syria. Sultan Baybars captured it in 1271.
castles.content:
In 1142 the Count of Tripoli gave a hilltop fort in western Syria to the Knights Hospitaller, a military order of the Crusades. Over the next century they turned it into Krak des Chevaliers, the "fortress of the knights", with two rings of thick walls and massive round towers.

The castle held out through many sieges. In 1271 the Mamluk sultan Baybars surrounded it, broke through the outer wall and, according to the chronicles, used a forged letter to persuade the knights to surrender. The Mamluks then repaired and strengthened it.

The young T. E. Lawrence, who studied it in 1909, called it perhaps the best preserved and most wholly admirable castle in the world. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006, together with the Citadel of Saladin.

castles.title: Citadel of Saladin, Cairo
castles.excerpt: Saladin began the Cairo Citadel in 1176 to defend the city against the Crusaders. For nearly seven centuries it was the seat of Egypt's rulers, and the Mosque of Muhammad Ali now crowns its skyline.
castles.content:
In 1176 Salah ad-Din, the sultan who would later retake Jerusalem, began a fortress on a spur of the Muqattam hills overlooking Cairo. He wanted a stronghold safe from the Crusaders and from rivals within the city. Its walls and towers were built partly with stones taken from small pyramids at Giza.

From the 13th century to the 19th century, the Citadel was the seat of government of Egypt, home to Mamluk sultans and Ottoman governors. In 1811 Muhammad Ali Pasha invited the Mamluk leaders to a feast here and had them killed, taking full control of Egypt.

Muhammad Ali then built the huge domed mosque, finished in 1848, that gives the Citadel its famous outline. The Citadel is part of Historic Cairo, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979.

castles.title: Arg-e Bam
castles.excerpt: Arg-e Bam was a whole fortified town of sun-dried mud brick, with houses, bazaars and a citadel on top. Almost destroyed by the earthquake of 2003, it is slowly being rebuilt.
castles.content:
In the desert of south-eastern Iran, the town of Bam grew rich on trade, dates and silk. Its fortified old town, the Arg-e Bam, may go back to the Achaemenid Persians, and it flourished between the 7th and 11th centuries on the trade routes between Persia, Central Asia and India.

Everything was built of mud brick and straw: the outer walls and towers, the houses and bazaars, the mosque and, at the very top, the governor's citadel. It was the largest adobe building complex in the world.

On 26 December 2003 a powerful earthquake struck Bam, killing more than 26,000 people and destroying much of the citadel. In 2004 UNESCO listed Bam and its Cultural Landscape as a World Heritage Site, and careful rebuilding is still going on.

castles.title: Tower of London
castles.excerpt: After conquering England in 1066, William the Conqueror built the White Tower beside the Thames to awe the people of London. Over nine centuries it has been a palace, a prison, a mint and the home of the Crown Jewels.
castles.content:
In 1066 William of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings and became king of England. To control London, he built a fortress beside the Thames, and around 1078 work began on the great stone keep we now call the White Tower.

Later kings surrounded it with two rings of walls and a moat. The Tower served as a royal palace, an armoury, the Royal Mint and a prison. Famous prisoners were held and some executed here, among them Queen Anne Boleyn in 1536.

Today it is guarded by the Yeoman Warders, nicknamed Beefeaters, and by a group of ravens: legend says that if the ravens ever leave, the kingdom will fall. The Crown Jewels are kept in the Jewel House, and the Tower has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

castles.title: Edinburgh Castle
castles.excerpt: Edinburgh Castle sits on Castle Rock, the plug of an ancient volcano, high above the Scottish capital. Its oldest building, St Margaret's Chapel, dates from the 12th century.
castles.content:
Castle Rock is the hard core of a volcano that died some 350 million years ago. With cliffs on three sides, it was a natural fortress, and people lived on it long before the castle. By the 12th century it was a royal castle of the kings of Scotland.

The oldest building in Edinburgh, St Margaret's Chapel, was built here around 1130. During the wars between Scotland and England, the castle changed hands again and again and was besieged many times.

Today it holds the Honours of Scotland, the oldest crown jewels in Britain, and the Stone of Destiny, returned to Scotland in 1996. The One O'Clock Gun has been fired from its walls since 1861. The castle is part of the Old and New Towns of Edinburgh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995.

castles.title: Alhambra
castles.excerpt: On a hill above Granada, the Nasrid sultans built the Alhambra, "the red one": a fortress outside and a dream of carved stucco, tiles and fountains inside. It was the last Muslim stronghold in Spain until 1492.
castles.content:
In 1238 Muhammad ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid dynasty, began building a fortress-palace on the Sabika hill above Granada. Its walls of reddish earth gave it its name, al-Hamra, "the red one". For over 250 years it was the heart of the last Muslim kingdom in Spain.

Behind its plain fortress walls, the sultans Yusuf I and Muhammad V created some of the most beautiful rooms in the world, covered with carved plaster, coloured tiles and Arabic poetry. The Court of the Lions, with its fountain held up by twelve stone lions, was built under Muhammad V in the 14th century.

On 2 January 1492, Sultan Muhammad XII, known as Boabdil, handed the keys of Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella. The Alhambra, with the gardens of the Generalife, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.

castles.title: Neuschwanstein Castle
castles.excerpt: King Ludwig II built Neuschwanstein as a romantic retreat inspired by medieval legends and Wagner's operas. It was never a real fortress, but it became the most famous castle image in the world.
castles.content:
King Ludwig II of Bavaria loved medieval legends and the operas of Richard Wagner. In 1869 he laid the foundation stone of a new castle on a crag above the Pöllat gorge, near the castle where he had spent his childhood.

Neuschwanstein looks like a knight's castle, but it was built with modern technology: it had central heating, running water and even a telephone. The king lived in it for only a few months. He died in mysterious circumstances in June 1886, before it was finished, and the castle opened to visitors just weeks later.

Its towers inspired Walt Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle. In 2025 it was listed by UNESCO as part of the Palaces of King Ludwig II of Bavaria.

castles.title: Cité de Carcassonne
castles.excerpt: Carcassonne's Cité is the largest walled medieval town in Europe, with two rings of walls and 52 towers on a hill in southern France. A 19th-century restoration saved it from demolition.
castles.content:
On a hill above the River Aude, the Romans built the first walls of Carcassonne. In the 12th century the Trencavel viscounts built the castle, the Château Comtal, and the town became a centre of the Cathars, a Christian movement the Church declared heretical.

In 1209 a crusade against the Cathars besieged Carcassonne and took it. The kings of France then added a second, outer ring of walls, making the Cité almost impossible to capture: about three kilometres of ramparts with 52 towers.

By the 19th century the walls were crumbling and the government planned to pull them down. Local people protested, and from 1853 the architect Viollet-le-Duc restored them, adding the pointed slate roofs we see today. The Cité became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.

castles.title: Himeji Castle
castles.excerpt: Himeji Castle's white walls and layered roofs look like a heron taking flight. Completed in its present form in 1609, it survived wars, bombing and earthquakes, and was Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage Site.
castles.content:
A fort first stood on Himeyama hill in the 14th century. In the 1580s the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi rebuilt it, and between 1601 and 1609 the lord Ikeda Terumasa turned it into the great castle complex we see today, with a six-storey main keep linked to three smaller ones.

Its brilliant white plaster walls and graceful roofs earned it the name Shirasagi-jo, the White Heron Castle. Behind the beauty is a clever defensive maze: winding paths, dead ends and gates designed to confuse attackers on their way to the keep.

Himeji survived the bombing of the city in 1945 and the great Kobe earthquake of 1995. In 1993 it became one of Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and a major restoration was completed in 2015.

castles.title: Osaka Castle
castles.excerpt: Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who unified Japan, began Osaka Castle in 1583 as the grandest castle of its age. It was destroyed in 1615, rebuilt by the Tokugawa, and its main keep was reconstructed in 1931.
castles.content:
In 1583 Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the warlord who brought all of Japan under his rule, began Osaka Castle on the site of a former temple-fortress. Its keep was decorated with gold leaf, and huge stone walls and moats surrounded it.

After Hideyoshi's death, Tokugawa Ieyasu besieged the castle in 1614 and 1615 and destroyed the Toyotomi family. The Tokugawa rebuilt the castle on an even larger scale, with some of the biggest stones ever used in a Japanese castle wall.

The keep burned after a lightning strike in 1665. The one we see today was rebuilt in 1931 with money given by the people of Osaka, and it houses a museum about Hideyoshi and the castle's history.
